Array.summary: The JavaScript `Array` object stores an ordered collection of values under one variable name. Arrays are zero-indexed, resizable, can mix value types, and provide methods for common collection operations.
Array.explanation: JavaScript's Array object represents an ordered, indexed collection. Arrays can resize, hold values of different types, and provide instance methods plus static helpers for common operations; indexing starts at zero, and standard copying operations produce shallow copies.
Array.syntax:
new Array(element0, element1, /* … , */ elementN)
Array(element0, element1, /* … , */ elementN)
[element0, element1, /* … , */ elementN]
Array.returns: Array instances are returned by the constructor and conversion helpers; individual members return operation-specific values.

example.title: Create, transform, and access an array
example.explanation: Creates an array, transforms each element into a new array, and accesses the first element by its zero-based index.

useCases.title: Collections
useCases.scenario: Represent an ordered sequence of values for iteration and indexed access.

useCases.title: Data processing
useCases.scenario: Transform or filter records while preserving a collection-oriented workflow.

useCases.title: Interoperability
useCases.scenario: Convert iterable or array-like input into a conventional JavaScript array.

interview.question: What is a JavaScript Array?
interview.answer: Array is an object representing a collection of multiple items under one variable name. It is zero-indexed, resizable, and may contain values of different types.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid shared nested state when copying an array? Use an explicit deep-copy strategy; ordinary array-copy operations are shallow.

interview.question: How are Array elements indexed?
interview.answer: The first element is at index 0, and the last element is at `length - 1`. Accessing an element uses bracket notation, such as `items[0]`.
interview.followUp: What happens when the requested index is outside the populated range? The result is `undefined`, rather than an associative lookup by an arbitrary string.

interview.question: Name two useful static Array methods.
interview.answer: `Array.from()` creates a new Array instance from an iterable or array-like object. `Array.isArray()` returns `true` for arrays and `false` otherwise.
interview.followUp: Why can `Array.from()` still leave nested objects shared? The resulting array is a shallow copy of the referenced values.

keyPoints: An Array can grow or shrink and can contain heterogeneous values such as numbers, strings, objects, and other arrays.
The first element uses index 0; subsequent elements increase the index by one.
For a nonempty array, the final element is found at `array.length - 1`.
Calling `Array()` or using array-literal syntax creates an Array object.
`Array.from()` converts supported iterable or array-like input into a new array.
`Array.isArray(value)` is the direct built-in test for whether a value is an Array.
gotchas: Do not use arbitrary strings as array indexes; array elements are accessed with nonnegative integer indexes or their string forms.
Copying an array does not recursively clone nested objects or arrays, so mutations inside shared nested values remain visible through both arrays.

Array.from.summary: Array.from() creates a new Array from an iterable or array-like object. An optional callback can transform each value as the result is built.
Array.from.explanation: Array.from() accepts an iterable or an array-like value, creates a new Array, and optionally transforms each source element with mapFn before placing it in the result. For array-like inputs, it uses indexed properties up to length; for iterable inputs, it follows iteration order.
Array.from.syntax:
Array.from(items)
Array.from(items, mapFn)
Array.from(items, mapFn, thisArg)

parameters.name: items
parameters.description: The iterable or array-like object to convert into an array.

parameters.name: mapFn
parameters.description: Optional function called for each element; its return value is stored in the result.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when invoking mapFn.

example.title: Convert and transform an iterable
example.explanation: Creates an array from the string and transforms each character during creation.

useCases.title: Materialize iterable values
useCases.scenario: Turn strings, Sets, Maps, or other iterables into ordinary arrays for indexed access and array methods.

useCases.title: Normalize array-like values
useCases.scenario: Convert DOM collections or custom objects with length and indexed properties into arrays.

useCases.title: Transform during creation
useCases.scenario: Apply a one-step conversion and transformation without a separate map pass.

interview.question: What does Array.from() do?
interview.answer: Array.from() creates a new shallow Array from an iterable or an array-like object. Its optional mapFn transforms values while the result is being built.
interview.followUp: How does it treat a string? A string is iterable, so characters are processed in iteration order rather than by enumerating ordinary object keys.

interview.question: How does Array.from() distinguish iterable and array-like inputs?
interview.answer: For an iterable, Array.from() follows the iterable's values. For an array-like object, it reads indexed properties according to the object's length.
interview.followUp: What happens when an array-like object lacks an indexed property? The corresponding result position contains undefined, keeping the result dense.

interview.question: How does the mapping callback work?
interview.answer: mapFn is optional and is called for each source element; its returned value is inserted into the new array. The callback receives the element and index, and thisArg can provide its this binding.
interview.followUp: Why prefer mapFn over Array.from(source).map(fn) when both work? It performs the transformation as the array is created and avoids requiring a separate intermediate array.

keyPoints: It is a static method that returns a separate, shallow copy rather than modifying the source.
The second argument can transform every element during construction.
The input may be an iterable such as a Set or a value exposing indexed properties and length.
The return value is a newly created Array.
The callback is invoked per element and also receives that element's index.
When called with a suitable constructor context, it can create instances through that constructor rather than being limited to ordinary Array construction.
Absent indexes in array-like input become explicit undefined elements.
gotchas: Missing indexed properties are represented by undefined rather than holes, so the result is always dense.
mapFn receives the current value and its index; use thisArg when the callback needs an explicit this value.
Array.from() does not consume asynchronous iterables; use Array.fromAsync() for that case.

Array.fromAsync.summary: Array.fromAsync() builds a new array from an async iterable, iterable, or array-like object. It returns a promise and awaits source values and optional mapping results.
Array.fromAsync.explanation: Array.fromAsync() consumes an async iterable, ordinary iterable, or array-like value and returns a promise for a new array. It awaits values from non-async sources and also awaits the result of an optional mapping function.
Array.fromAsync.syntax:
Array.fromAsync(items)
Array.fromAsync(items, mapFn)
Array.fromAsync(items, mapFn, thisArg)

parameters.name: items
parameters.type: async iterable, iterable, or array-like object
parameters.description: An async iterable, iterable, or array-like object to convert to an array.

parameters.name: mapFn
parameters.description: Optional function called for every element; its returned value is awaited and added to the result.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when executing mapFn.

Array.fromAsync.returns: A Promise fulfilled with a new Array instance.

example.title: Await asynchronous mapping results
example.explanation: The mapping function runs for each input and its result is awaited before the resulting array is fulfilled.

useCases.title: Materialize asynchronous streams
useCases.scenario: Collect values produced over time by an async generator or another async iterable.

useCases.title: Normalize asynchronous or iterable data
useCases.scenario: Convert Set, Map, or indexed array-like data while resolving promise-valued elements.

useCases.title: Build arrays with async mapping
useCases.scenario: Apply asynchronous transformation logic while collecting results into an array.

interview.question: What does Array.fromAsync() return?
interview.answer: It returns a promise whose fulfillment value is a new Array instance. The source may be async iterable, iterable, or array-like.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from Array.from()? Array.fromAsync() supports async iterables and awaits values, whereas Array.from() returns the array synchronously.

interview.question: Which input kinds does it accept?
interview.answer: The first argument can be an async iterable, an ordinary iterable, or an array-like object. This lets it collect values from sources such as async generators, Set, Map, or indexed objects.
interview.followUp: What happens when a source is both async and synchronous iterable? The async-iterable handling takes precedence.

interview.question: How do mapFn and thisArg work?
interview.answer: mapFn is called for each element, and its return value is awaited before it is placed in the resulting array. thisArg optionally supplies the this value used while calling mapFn.
interview.followUp: Are synchronous-source values passed to mapFn as unresolved promises? No; those values are awaited first, so mapFn receives the resolved elements.

keyPoints: The method creates a fresh shallow array rather than modifying the source.
Its input may follow asynchronous iteration, synchronous iteration, or indexed array-like access.
The operation is asynchronous at the API boundary: callers receive a promise for the collected array.
Values from non-async sources are resolved before the mapping step processes them.
Values yielded by an async iterable are supplied directly to the mapper after async iteration obtains them.
The mapper receives the current element being processed.
gotchas: For synchronous iterables and array-like inputs, values are awaited before mapping receives them.
An asynchronous mapper is supported, but its result is resolved before insertion into the output array.

Array.of.summary: Array.of() creates a new array from its arguments, regardless of how many arguments there are or what types they have. A single number is stored as an element, unlike with Array().
Array.of.explanation: Array.of() creates and returns a new Array containing its arguments in order. Unlike the Array constructor, one numeric argument becomes an element rather than an array length; the method can also be inherited by array subclasses or called with another suitable constructor.
Array.of.syntax:
Array.of()
Array.of(element1)
Array.of(element1, element2)
Array.of(element1, element2, /* …, */ elementN)

parameters.name: element1, …, elementN
parameters.description: The values to place into the newly created array, in argument order.

example.title: Creating arrays from arguments
example.explanation: The method creates arrays whose elements are exactly the supplied arguments, including when there is one argument or none.

useCases.title: Consistent array construction
useCases.scenario: Build an array from a dynamic argument list without special handling for a single numeric value.

useCases.title: Single-value arrays
useCases.scenario: Create a one-element array containing a number, including zero or another length-like value.

useCases.title: Subclass-aware factories
useCases.scenario: Use an inherited static factory when an Array subclass should receive the result.

interview.question: What does Array.of() do?
interview.answer: Array.of() is a static factory that returns a new Array containing all supplied arguments in order. It also supports zero arguments and preserves each argument as an element.
interview.followUp: What does Array.of(7) return compared with Array(7)? Array.of(7) returns [7], whereas Array(7) creates an array with length 7 and empty slots.

interview.question: How does Array.of() differ from Array()?
interview.answer: Array.of(7) treats 7 as the first element, so the result is [7]. Array(7) interprets the single numeric argument as the desired length and creates empty slots instead.
interview.followUp: What happens with Array.of(undefined)? It returns an array containing one element whose value is undefined.

interview.question: Why is Array.of() described as a generic factory method?
interview.answer: The method is generic and uses its this value as the constructor for the result. An inherited call can therefore create an instance of an Array subclass, provided the constructor accepts the length argument used by the method.
interview.followUp: Can any constructor be used? Yes, the documentation says the this value can be any constructor function that accepts one argument representing the new array's length.

keyPoints: It is a static method that constructs a fresh array from any number of supplied arguments.
Each parameter is an element placed into the resulting array.
The return value is a newly created Array.
A single numeric argument remains an array element instead of being interpreted as a length.
Multiple arguments appear in the output array in the same order.
Undefined is retained as an actual array element.
gotchas: Do not substitute Array(7) when you mean an array containing the number 7: Array.of(7) produces [7], while Array(7) creates empty slots and sets length to 7.
When inherited by an Array subclass, the result is an instance of that subclass rather than a plain Array.

ArrayBuffer.summary: ArrayBuffer represents raw binary storage as a sequence of bytes. Access its contents through a typed-array view or DataView; it can also be created as resizable and transferred between execution contexts.
ArrayBuffer.explanation: An ArrayBuffer owns a region of raw bytes but does not provide direct element access. Use a typed-array view or DataView to interpret and modify those bytes; optionally create the buffer as resizable and later change its byte length.

parameters.name: byteLength
parameters.description: The initial buffer length in bytes.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional construction settings, including maxByteLength for a resizable buffer.

example.title: Create and resize a buffer
example.explanation: Creates a resizable buffer, writes bytes through a typed-array view, expands the buffer, and prints the resulting bytes.

useCases.title: Binary data processing
useCases.scenario: Parsing or constructing binary formats such as protocol messages and file headers.

useCases.title: Cross-context data transfer
useCases.scenario: Passing byte storage between workers or other execution contexts.

useCases.title: Resizable storage
useCases.scenario: Managing memory whose required capacity can grow within a known upper bound.

interview.question: What is an ArrayBuffer, and how do you read its contents?
interview.answer: ArrayBuffer represents raw binary storage as bytes. It does not itself define how those bytes are interpreted, so code uses a typed-array view or DataView for access.
interview.followUp: How would you share the same bytes between two numeric interpretations? Create multiple views over the same ArrayBuffer, choosing the element types and offsets needed.

interview.question: How do resizable ArrayBuffers work?
interview.answer: Pass maxByteLength in the constructor options to create a resizable buffer. Its current size can then be changed with resize(), while resizable and maxByteLength report its capabilities and limit.
interview.followUp: What happens when a resizable buffer is shortened below a view's range? The view's accessible range is adjusted according to the buffer's new byte length.

interview.question: What happens when an ArrayBuffer is transferred?
interview.answer: ArrayBuffer is transferable between execution contexts through the structured clone algorithm. Transfer copies the bytes into a new buffer and detaches the original buffer.
interview.followUp: How can a fixed-length destination be requested when transferring? Use transferToFixedLength() rather than transfer().

keyPoints: Use new ArrayBuffer(length) to allocate a fixed-length buffer with the requested byte count.
Typed arrays and DataView provide the format-specific access layer for an ArrayBuffer.
Providing maxByteLength when constructing the buffer enables later resizing up to that maximum.
Call resize(newLength) to change the byte length of a resizable buffer.
gotchas: An ArrayBuffer has no direct element access; use a typed-array view or DataView to read and write its contents.

AsyncGenerator.summary: AsyncGenerator is the object produced by calling an async generator function. It is both an async iterable and async iterator, and its methods return promises.
AsyncGenerator.explanation: An AsyncGenerator is the object produced whenever an async generator function is called. It is both asynchronously iterable and an async iterator: its next(), throw(), and return() operations produce promises, while the generator can pause at yield and resume around awaited work.
AsyncGenerator.returns: An object returned by an async generator function that conforms to both the async iterable and async iterator protocols; its generator methods return promises.

example.title: Consume an async generator
example.explanation: Calling an async generator creates an AsyncGenerator. The loop requests values through next(), awaits each promise, and stops when done is true.

useCases.title: Lazy asynchronous streams
useCases.scenario: Stream values produced over time without loading the complete sequence first.

useCases.title: Paginated or event-driven work
useCases.scenario: Combine await-based operations with incremental yield of results.

useCases.title: for await...of pipelines
useCases.scenario: Consume asynchronous sequences with automatic awaiting and completion handling.

interview.question: What is an AsyncGenerator?
interview.answer: An AsyncGenerator is returned by an async generator function. It implements both the async iterable and async iterator protocols, and its iterator methods return promises.
interview.followUp: How is it normally consumed? Use for await...of, which repeatedly requests and awaits iterator results until the result object's done property is true.

interview.question: What does AsyncGenerator.prototype.next() return?
interview.answer: Calling next() requests the next sequence result and returns a promise. The fulfilled value is an iterator-result object containing value and done, where done indicates whether execution has finished.
interview.followUp: What does passing an argument to next() do? The value is delivered to the suspended yield expression, allowing the generator to receive input when it resumes.

interview.question: How do throw() and return() affect an async generator?
interview.answer: throw() behaves as though a throw statement were inserted at the generator's currently suspended position. The generator may catch the error, continue yielding, or remain rejected if the error is uncaught.
interview.followUp: How does return() differ? It injects a return at the suspended position, finishes the generator, and permits cleanup in a finally block.

keyPoints: Calling an async generator function creates the AsyncGenerator instance.
The same object can supply an async iterator and be consumed as an async iterable.
Operations such as next(), throw(), and return() complete asynchronously through promises.
Its prototype relationship includes the hidden AsyncIterator base class.
AsyncGenerator objects are produced by async generator functions rather than by a public constructor.
The shared prototype is internal and is used by objects created from async generator functions.
gotchas: Do not instantiate AsyncGenerator directly; obtain instances by calling an async generator function.
Iterator operations are asynchronous, so handle their results as promises or consume the object with for await...of.

AsyncIterator.summary: AsyncIterator is an object whose next() method returns a promise for an iterator result. Built-in async iterators inherit from AsyncIterator.prototype, which makes them usable as async iterables.
AsyncIterator.explanation: AsyncIterator describes objects whose next() method returns a promise for an iterator result. Built-in async iterators inherit from AsyncIterator.prototype, whose Symbol.asyncIterator method returns the iterator itself so it can also be used as an async iterable.

example.title: Consume an async iterator
example.explanation: An async generator produces an AsyncIterator, which can be consumed directly by a for await...of loop.

useCases.title: Asynchronous sequences
useCases.scenario: Consume values produced over time, such as results from an async generator.

useCases.title: Streaming consumption
useCases.scenario: Process stream-like data with for await...of while each value becomes available.

useCases.title: Custom async iteration
useCases.scenario: Implement a custom object that exposes asynchronous next() operations.

interview.question: What is an AsyncIterator?
interview.answer: An AsyncIterator is an object whose next() method returns a promise that fulfills with an iterator result. Its prototype also supplies Symbol.asyncIterator(), allowing the object to be consumed as an async iterable.
interview.followUp: How is it normally consumed? Use for await...of, which obtains the async iterator through Symbol.asyncIterator() and awaits each result from next().

interview.question: What does Symbol.asyncIterator do on AsyncIterator.prototype?
interview.answer: AsyncIterator.prototype[Symbol.asyncIterator]() returns the current iterator object. This makes an async iterator also satisfy the async iterable protocol without creating a separate wrapper.
interview.followUp: Why does this matter in practice? Syntax such as for await...of can call the method automatically and iterate the same object.

interview.question: How do async generators relate to AsyncIterator?
interview.answer: Async generator functions return AsyncIterator objects. Those objects can be passed directly to for await...of, which repeatedly awaits next() until the returned result has done set to true.
interview.followUp: Can for await...of consume synchronous iterables too? Yes; if no async iterator exists, it falls back to a synchronous iterator and wraps its results asynchronously.

keyPoints: An AsyncIterator supplies next(), and calling it produces a promise rather than an immediate iterator result.
The promise from next() fulfills with an iterator result, typically containing value and done properties.
The prototype makes the iterator async iterable by returning the same object from Symbol.asyncIterator().
Because it is also async iterable, the object works with language constructs that expect an async iterable.
Concrete async iterator kinds can define their own next() behavior on distinct prototypes.
A for await...of loop is the standard syntax for consuming built-in async iterators asynchronously.
gotchas: AsyncIterator is not typically obtained by directly constructing a value; built-in async iterators inherit from its prototype.
In core JavaScript, async generators are the main built-in source of AsyncIterator objects; other examples may come from web APIs.

at.summary: Array.prototype.at() returns the element at a given integer index and supports negative indexes that count from the end. It returns undefined when the index is outside the array's bounds.
at.explanation: Call at(index) on an array to read one element. The index is converted to an integer; non-negative values count from the beginning, while negative values are added to the array length so they count backward from the end. An index outside the array produces undefined.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: A zero-based index, converted to an integer. Negative values count from the end of the array.

at.returns: The element at the selected index, or undefined when the index is outside the array's bounds.

example.title: Read array elements with relative indexes
example.code:
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];

console.log(colors.at(0));  // "red"
console.log(colors.at(-1)); // "blue"
console.log(colors.at(99)); // undefined
example.explanation: Use a non-negative index for ordinary access and a negative index to count from the end.

useCases.title: Access from the end
useCases.scenario: Read the most recent item without manually subtracting from length.

useCases.title: Index-based access
useCases.scenario: Use a concise, readable alternative to array[index] for ordinary element lookup.

useCases.title: Work with array-like data
useCases.scenario: Read values from objects that expose length and integer-keyed properties.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.at() do?
interview.answer: at(index) returns the element at a zero-based index. Negative indexes count backward from the array's end, so at(-1) returns the final element; an out-of-range index returns undefined.
interview.followUp: How does at() differ from bracket notation for negative indexes? Bracket notation treats -1 as the string property "-1", whereas at(-1) performs relative indexing.

interview.question: How are positive and negative indexes interpreted?
interview.answer: For a non-negative integer, at(index) is equivalent to array[index]. Its distinctive feature is that a negative index is translated relative to the array length.
interview.followUp: What happens for a fractional index? The argument is converted to an integer before the element lookup.

interview.question: Is at() limited to Array instances?
interview.answer: The method is generic: it needs a this value with a length property and integer-keyed properties. Therefore, it can read from suitable array-like objects, not only actual arrays.
interview.followUp: Can it be used on a typed array? TypedArray.prototype.at() has the same algorithm, but the typed-array method itself is not generic.

keyPoints: at() reads and returns the element selected by an integer index.
A negative index selects relative to the array's end; -1 means the final element.
Indexes are zero-based and the supplied value is converted to an integer.
For non-negative integer indexes, at() and bracket notation select the same element.
The method can operate on array-like objects that provide the required indexed structure.
Lookup uses the receiver's length to calculate the actual property index.
gotchas: Bracket notation does not support relative negative indexing: array[-1] reads the property named "-1", not the last element.
Out-of-range indexes return undefined, and the corresponding property is not accessed.

Atomics.summary: Atomics is a namespace of static methods for atomic operations on typed-array elements, including shared-memory synchronization. It is commonly used with SharedArrayBuffer to coordinate concurrent agents safely.
Atomics.explanation: Atomics is a namespace of static methods for indivisible operations on integer typed-array elements, especially when storage is shared between agents. Read-modify-write methods return the value that was present before the operation, while load, store, wait, and notification methods support coordination.
Atomics.syntax:
Atomics.add(typedArray, index, value)
Atomics.and(typedArray, index, value)
Atomics.compareExchange(typedArray, index, expectedValue, replacementValue)
Atomics.exchange(typedArray, index, value)
Atomics.isLockFree(size)
Atomics.load(typedArray, index)
Atomics.notify(typedArray, index, count)
Atomics.or(typedArray, index, value)
Atomics.store(typedArray, index, value)
Atomics.sub(typedArray, index, value)
Atomics.wait(typedArray, index, value, timeout)
Atomics.waitAsync(typedArray, index, value, timeout)
Atomics.xor(typedArray, index, value)

parameters.name: typedArray
parameters.description: An integer typed array, such as Int32Array or BigInt64Array, whose element is accessed atomically.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: The zero-based element position to access.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The operation-specific operand, such as a value to add, store, exchange, or compare.

parameters.name: expectedValue
parameters.description: For compareExchange, the value that must currently be present before replacement.

parameters.name: replacementValue
parameters.description: For compareExchange, the value written when the expected value matches.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: For wait and waitAsync, the value expected at the location before waiting.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: For wait and waitAsync, the maximum wait duration in milliseconds.

Atomics.returns: The result depends on the static method: read-modify-write methods generally return the old element value; load returns the current value; wait returns a status string; notify returns the number of awakened agents; waitAsync returns an object describing an immediate result or Promise.

example.title: Atomic counter update
example.explanation: This creates shared integer storage, atomically adds to one element, and reads both the previous and current values.

useCases.title: Shared counters
useCases.scenario: Several workers increment a shared counter without lost updates.

useCases.title: Thread synchronization
useCases.scenario: Workers coordinate progress through a shared state value.

useCases.title: Lock-free algorithms
useCases.scenario: A lock implementation needs indivisible compare-and-swap behavior.

useCases.title: Shared flags
useCases.scenario: A program needs atomic bitwise flags in shared integer storage.

interview.question: What problem does Atomics solve?
interview.answer: Atomics provides static methods that perform atomic operations on typed-array elements. These operations prevent another write from interleaving during the indivisible operation, which makes shared-memory updates predictable.
interview.followUp: Why is Atomics.add useful for a counter? It combines reading the old value, adding, and writing the result into one atomic operation, returning the old value.

interview.question: How is Atomics used?
interview.answer: Atomics is a namespace object, not a constructor, so it cannot be used with new. Its methods are called directly, such as Atomics.load(array, index) or Atomics.store(array, index, value).
interview.followUp: How does this differ from Math? Both expose static operations, but Atomics operates on integer typed-array elements and supports shared-memory synchronization.

interview.question: What are Atomics.wait and Atomics.notify for?
interview.answer: The wait and notify methods allow agents to coordinate through a shared-memory location. wait checks the value and can block until notification or timeout, while notify wakes agents waiting at an index.
interview.followUp: When should waitAsync be preferred? It is non-blocking and can be used on the main thread, returning either an immediate result or a Promise.

keyPoints: Atomics is a namespace rather than an instance-based API; all operations are exposed as static methods.
The methods operate on typed-array views backed by shared or ordinary array buffers.
Atomic access prevents an operation's read and write phases from being interrupted by another write.
Atomics.add performs an atomic addition at one typed-array position.
Read-modify-write methods such as add, sub, and exchange return the element's pre-operation value.
Atomics.notify wakes agents waiting on a selected shared-memory index.
gotchas: Do not call Atomics with new or invoke it as a function; use its static methods directly.
Atomic operations require an allowed integer typed array, not an arbitrary typed-array view.
wait and notify are synchronization primitives; use them for coordination rather than ordinary value updates.

BigInt.summary: BigInt(value) converts a supported value into a primitive BigInt. It accepts integer-like values, strings, booleans, and BigInts, but rejects fractional Numbers and cannot be called with new.
BigInt.explanation: Call BigInt(value) without new to convert a supported value into a bigint primitive. Strings are parsed as integer-literal text, booleans become 1n or 0n, and Number inputs must be integral; fractional Numbers, invalid strings, and unsupported values throw.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to convert; it may be a string, an integer, a boolean, or another BigInt.

example.title: Convert values to BigInt
example.explanation: Converts an integer Number and a binary-prefixed string into BigInt primitives.

useCases.title: Parse integer strings
useCases.scenario: Converting user or configuration text such as "0x123" into an exact integer representation.

useCases.title: Convert integral Numbers
useCases.scenario: Turning an integral Number into a BigInt when subsequent calculations require bigint values.

useCases.title: Convert booleans
useCases.scenario: Mapping boolean flags to numeric BigInt values for bigint-based logic.

interview.question: What does BigInt() do?
interview.answer: BigInt(value) returns a primitive whose type is bigint. It accepts values such as strings, integers, booleans, and existing BigInts, and it must be called without new.
interview.followUp: What happens with BigInt(1.2)? It throws RangeError because Number input must be integral.

interview.question: Which Number values can BigInt() convert?
interview.answer: A decimal integer Number can be converted, but a non-integral Number throws RangeError. Conversion is explicit, so this is the documented route for converting an integer Number to BigInt.
interview.followUp: Why can conversion alter a large Number? Number may already have lost precision before BigInt receives it; use a string or BigInt literal when exactness matters.

interview.question: How are strings handled?
interview.answer: A string is interpreted using integer-literal syntax. Leading and trailing whitespace are allowed, and binary, octal, and hexadecimal prefixes can be used; an unparseable string throws SyntaxError.
interview.followUp: What does BigInt("0x123") produce? It produces 291n, because the string is parsed as hexadecimal integer-literal text.

keyPoints: The result is a primitive bigint, not a wrapper object.
The conversion input can be a supported string, integral Number, boolean, or BigInt.

interview.question: How is byte order controlled?

interview.followUp: Can a DataView read unaligned values? Yes; multi-byte values can be accessed from any in-bounds byte offset.

interview.question: What does a JavaScript Date store?
interview.answer: A Date represents one instant using milliseconds from the UTC epoch, 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. The timestamp itself is independent of time zone.
interview.followUp: How do you detect an invalid Date? Use Number.isNaN(date.getTime()), because invalid dates have a NaN timestamp.

interview.question: How do Date() and new Date() differ?
interview.answer: new Date() constructs a Date object for the current instant. Date() without new instead returns a string for the current date and time, and supplied arguments to the function form are ignored.
interview.followUp: What does new Date(0) represent? It represents the epoch instant, midnight at the beginning of January 1, 1970 UTC.

interview.question: How do local and UTC Date methods differ?
interview.answer: Methods beginning with getUTC interpret calendar fields in universal time, while methods such as getDate() interpret them in local time. Both operate on the same underlying timestamp.
interview.followUp: Why can local calendar fields differ from UTC fields? The host environment's local time zone may place the instant on a different date or clock time.

Its core value is an integer count of elapsed milliseconds from the UTC epoch.
getTime() reads the timestamp, while setTime() replaces it and changes the represented instant.
Date.now() provides the current epoch timestamp without creating a Date object.

interview.question: What does String.prototype.endsWith() return?
interview.answer: It returns a boolean indicating whether the string ends with the characters in searchString. The default endpoint is the string length, and an empty search string returns true.
interview.followUp: What does the second argument do? It supplies the endpoint used for the comparison, so the method tests the substring ending at that position rather than necessarily the full string.

interview.question: How does endsWith() handle the search argument?
interview.answer: The first argument is converted to a string unless it is a regular expression. A regular expression causes a TypeError instead of being accepted as a pattern.
interview.followUp: Why does a regex throw? The method is designed for string matching, and the API explicitly rejects regex arguments.

interview.question: How does endPosition affect the result?
interview.answer: endPosition is the position at which the searched text is expected to finish, with a default of str.length. Values outside the string's range are effectively bounded to the valid range.
interview.followUp: What happens when the endpoint is too early for the search string? The method returns false because the requested search text cannot fit before that endpoint.

The optional second argument chooses where the searched text must finish.
Without an endpoint, the comparison reaches the end of the complete string.
An empty search string always produces true.
Numbers, booleans, and other non-regex values are converted before comparison.
The comparison distinguishes letter case.

interview.question: What does the Error constructor do, and is new required?

interview.question: What does `Array.prototype.every()` return?
interview.answer: `every()` returns a boolean. It returns `false` immediately when the predicate is falsy for an element; otherwise it returns `true` after all applicable elements pass.
interview.followUp: What happens with `[]`? It returns `true`, which corresponds to the universal condition having no counterexample.

interview.question: What arguments can the predicate receive?

A predicate is invoked for each eligible element, in traversal order.
Failure short-circuits the scan, avoiding unnecessary later callback calls.
Only present indexes are tested; absent sparse-array entries are ignored.
The method can be borrowed by array-like values with the required indexed structure.
A borrowed call needs a length and integer-indexed properties.

Holes in sparse arrays are skipped rather than passed to the callback, so they cannot directly cause failure.

interview.question: What does fetch() return, and when does its promise fulfill?
interview.answer: fetch() returns a Promise that fulfills with a Response when the response is available, specifically after the server responds with headers. The Response represents the request result and its body can then be consumed with methods such as json().
interview.followUp: How should an HTTP 404 be handled? Check response.ok or status after fulfillment, because HTTP error statuses do not by themselves reject the fetch promise.

interview.question: What arguments can fetch() receive?
interview.answer: The first argument identifies the resource and may be a URL-like input or a Request. An optional initialization object configures request details such as method, headers, and body.
interview.followUp: What happens when options overlap with those in a Request? Values supplied directly to fetch() take precedence.

interview.question: Does fetch() reject for HTTP errors?
interview.answer: fetch() is available as a global method in Window and worker contexts. Its promise rejects for network failures, but an HTTP error response normally still fulfills the promise, so application code must inspect the Response.
interview.followUp: How can the response payload be decoded? Call the appropriate Response body method, such as json() or text(), after checking the status.

Browser window code and worker code can call the same global function.
The resource input is required; an optional second argument customizes the request.
The result is asynchronous and provides a Response object rather than the payload directly.
The promise can fulfill before the complete response body has been downloaded.
Read metadata such as status from Response, then consume its body separately.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.fill() do?
interview.answer: fill() writes one value across an array index range and returns the modified array. The start index is inclusive, while the end index is exclusive.
interview.followUp: What happens with negative bounds? They are interpreted relative to the array's end and then constrained to valid positions.

interview.question: Does fill() mutate the array or alter its length?
interview.answer: The method mutates the receiver but does not change its length. If no bounds are supplied, it fills from index 0 through the final index.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid mutation? Create a shallow copy first, such as [...array], and call fill() on that copy.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.find() return, and when does it stop?
interview.answer: find() calls the predicate in ascending index order and stops as soon as the predicate returns a truthy value. It returns that element; if no predicate call succeeds, it returns undefined.

interview.question: What arguments can the find() callback receive?

interview.followUp: How does it differ from `find()`? `find()` returns the matching element itself, whereas `findIndex()` returns its numeric position.

interview.question: What arguments does the callback receive?
interview.answer: The callback receives the current element, its index, and the array on which `findIndex()` was called. A truthy callback result indicates a match; a falsy result continues the search.
interview.followUp: How can callback context be supplied? Pass a second argument as `thisArg`; it becomes the callback's `this` value when the callback is invoked.

interview.question: What happens when no element satisfies the predicate?
interview.answer: If no callback invocation returns a truthy value, the method returns `-1`. This distinguishes “not found” from a valid zero-based index, including index `0`.
interview.followUp: Can it be used on array-like objects? Yes: the method is generic and only requires a `length` property plus integer-keyed properties.

keyPoints: It identifies the first matching element by position rather than returning the element itself.
Evaluation follows increasing numeric indexes.
The operation short-circuits at the first truthy test result.
The predicate can inspect the current value.
The predicate can make its decision using the current position.
The callback can access the complete receiver array.
It can operate on suitable array-like objects, not only actual Array instances.
gotchas: A non-match is represented by `-1`, so do not treat the returned number as a valid index without checking it.

flat.summary: `Array.prototype.flat()` creates a new array by recursively concatenating nested arrays up to a chosen depth. Without an argument, it flattens one level.
flat.explanation: Calling `flat()` creates a new array by concatenating nested array elements up to the requested depth. The default depth is 1; non-array elements are copied directly, and the original array is not changed.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: The depth level specifying how deeply nested arrays should be flattened. Defaults to 1.

flat.returns: A new array with sub-array elements concatenated into it.

example.title: Flatten nested arrays
example.explanation: The first call flattens one nesting level; the second flattens two levels.

useCases.title: Flatten one level
useCases.scenario: Turn arrays of arrays into a single-level array.

useCases.title: Flatten multiple levels
useCases.scenario: Normalize data nested at a known depth.

useCases.title: Use the generic method
useCases.scenario: Process array-like objects that expose length and integer-indexed properties.

keyPoints: `flat()` returns a new array containing nested elements concatenated through the specified depth.
The depth controls how many nested array levels are recursively flattened.
Omitting the depth argument flattens one level.
The return value is always a new array.
The original array remains unchanged, while object references in the result remain shallowly copied.
The method can operate on array-like values with a length and integer-indexed properties.
gotchas: Sparse arrays lose empty slots at the levels being flattened; deeper nested arrays retain their holes until those levels are flattened.
`flat()` does not mutate the source array; it returns a new shallow-copy array.
When called generically on array-like objects, only elements that are arrays are flattened.

flatMap.summary: Array.prototype.flatMap() maps each array element and flattens each callback result by one level. It returns a new array and does not recursively flatten deeper nesting.
flatMap.explanation: Call flatMap() on an array with a callback. JavaScript invokes the callback for each present element, appends a non-array result directly, or appends the elements of an array result after flattening that result by one level; it returns a new array rather than changing the source array.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: A function to execute for each element in the array. It should return an array containing new elements of the new array, or a single non-array value to be added to the new array.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: A value to use as this when executing callbackFn.

flatMap.returns: A new array with each element being the result of the callback function and flattened by a depth of 1.

example.title: Map and expand values
example.explanation: Each callback result contributes its elements to the new array, flattened by one level.

useCases.title: Expand or discard items
useCases.scenario: Convert each source item into zero, one, or several output items in one pass.

useCases.title: Flatten mapped records
useCases.scenario: Turn nested collections such as each object's list of records into one flat result.

useCases.title: Filter during mapping
useCases.scenario: Keep only matching values by returning an empty array for nonmatches.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.flatMap() do?
interview.answer: flatMap() applies a callback to each present array element and flattens each returned array by one level into a new array. It is equivalent in behavior to map() followed by flat(1), with the combined operation generally being more efficient.
interview.followUp: What happens when the callback returns a string or Set? They are appended as single values because only returned arrays are flattened.

interview.question: What arguments does the callback receive, and what may it return?
interview.answer: The callback receives the current element, its index, and the source array, as with map(). A returned array contributes its elements; a non-array return value contributes one element.
interview.followUp: Does changing the source array during iteration change the number of callback invocations? No: flatMap() reads the initial length and visits integer-indexed properties below that length.

interview.question: Can flatMap() be used with array-like objects?
interview.answer: flatMap() is generic: its this value needs a length property and integer-keyed properties. The callback's result is flattened only when that result is an Array.
interview.followUp: Can it flatten a custom iterable? No. A custom iterable is appended as one value unless it is itself an Array.

keyPoints: It maps each source element and produces a separate result array.
Nested callback results are reduced by exactly one array level, not recursively.
Its conceptual equivalent is arr.map(callback).flat(1).
The callback is processed element by element rather than receiving the whole array at once.
The method can operate on suitable array-like objects, not only actual Array instances.
Iteration uses the receiver's length and integer-indexed properties.
gotchas: Sparse source entries are skipped, so a hole does not invoke the callback.
Only arrays are flattened; returned iterables or array-like objects remain single values.

forEach.summary: Array.prototype.forEach() invokes a callback once for each assigned array element in ascending-index order. It returns undefined and is mainly used to perform side effects.
forEach.explanation: Call forEach with a callback to process array elements in ascending index order. The callback receives the current element, its index, and the source array; forEach returns undefined, so use it for side effects rather than producing a transformed array.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: A function invoked once for each assigned array element. It receives element, index, and array arguments; its return value is discarded.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when callbackFn executes.

example.title: Iterate and perform a side effect
example.explanation: Adds each price to an accumulator while demonstrating the optional thisArg.

useCases.title: Process every element
useCases.scenario: Logging, displaying, or otherwise handling each item individually.

useCases.title: Perform side effects
useCases.scenario: Updating external state or an accumulator during traversal.

useCases.title: Work with array-like values
useCases.scenario: Applying an operation to an array-like object that has length and integer-keyed properties.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.forEach return, and what arguments does its callback receive?
interview.answer: forEach invokes the callback once for each assigned array element, in ascending-index order. The callback receives the element, index, and array, and the method itself returns undefined.
interview.followUp: How would you create a transformed array instead? Use map(), whose callback results form a new array; forEach is intended for side effects.

interview.question: How does the optional thisArg parameter work?
interview.answer: The optional thisArg supplies the this value used when invoking the callback. This is useful with a traditional function; an arrow function has lexical this and does not take its this from thisArg.
interview.followUp: What happens if the callback is async? forEach does not wait for promises, so use an explicit loop when sequential awaiting is required.

interview.question: When should forEach be preferred over map()?
interview.answer: forEach is an iterative method for performing an action on each array element, not for constructing a result. It always returns undefined and therefore cannot be chained as a transformation.
interview.followUp: Can iteration be stopped normally? No; forEach has no break mechanism, so use a loop or a method such as some(), every(), or find() when early termination is needed.

keyPoints: It runs one callback invocation per assigned element in the array.
Traversal follows increasing numeric indexes rather than an arbitrary order.
The first callback argument is the currently visited value.
The callback’s second argument identifies the current element’s numeric position.
The third callback argument is the array on which iteration began.
The method can operate on array-like objects with length and integer-keyed properties when called appropriately.
Any value returned by the callback is ignored, so callbacks are used for actions rather than collecting results.
gotchas: A callback cannot terminate iteration with break or a special return value; throwing is the documented escape route.
Holes in a sparse array are skipped instead of causing callback invocations.
An async callback is not awaited, so asynchronous work can continue after forEach has returned.

Function.sourceTitle: Function() constructor - JavaScript - MDN Web Docs
Function.summary: The Function() constructor dynamically creates a callable Function object from parameter names and a function-body string. It runs in the global scope rather than capturing the local scope where it was created.
Function.explanation: The Function constructor builds a new function by treating every argument except the last as a parameter name and the final argument as the function body. The resulting function is parsed at construction time and runs with access only to its own scope and global scope, not the local scope where it was created.
Function.syntax:
new Function(functionBody)
new Function(arg1, functionBody)
new Function(arg1, arg2, functionBody)
new Function(arg1, arg2, /* …, */ argN, functionBody)
Function(functionBody)
Function(arg1, functionBody)
Function(arg1, arg2, functionBody)
Function(arg1, arg2, /* …, */ argN, functionBody)

parameters.name: arg1 … argN
parameters.description: One or more strings naming the function parameters; each argument before the final argument contributes a parameter name.

parameters.name: functionBody
parameters.description: JavaScript statements forming the function body; it may be a string or TrustedScript.

example.title: Create a function dynamically
example.code:
const multiply = new Function("a", "b", "return a * b");
console.log(multiply(3, 4)); // 12
example.explanation: Creates a function from parameter names and a function-body string, then invokes it.

useCases.title: Runtime-generated functions
useCases.scenario: Generate executable behavior from code supplied at runtime in a controlled environment.

useCases.title: Programmatic function assembly
useCases.scenario: Build a callable function when parameter names and implementation text are produced programmatically.

interview.question: How does the Function constructor interpret its arguments?
interview.answer: Function() creates a new Function object from strings. Arguments before the final one become parameter names, while the final argument becomes the function body.
interview.followUp: What happens if it is called without new? It has the same effect: both forms create a new Function instance.

interview.question: How does its scope differ from eval?
interview.answer: Unlike eval, a function created this way executes only in the global scope. It therefore cannot access local bindings from the constructor's surrounding scope.
interview.followUp: Can it access variables declared inside itself? Yes; its own parameters and local declarations remain available during execution.

interview.question: Why is the Function constructor usually discouraged?
interview.answer: The constructor parses the supplied function when the Function object is created. Static declarations and expressions are generally more efficient because they are parsed with the surrounding code.
interview.followUp: What is the main security concern? Untrusted input can become executable JavaScript, so dynamic construction should be avoided for such input.

keyPoints: It creates a new callable Function object from supplied strings.
Every argument except the final one supplies a parameter name, in order.
The function body may be supplied as a string or TrustedScript value.
Calling Function() and using new Function() produce the same kind of instance.
Constructed functions do not capture the lexical environment where construction occurs.
At runtime, access is limited to the function's own locals and global bindings.
gotchas: Never pass untrusted strings to the constructor: its inputs are parsed and executed as code, creating an injection and potential XSS risk.
Prefer a function declaration or expression for static code because dynamically constructed functions incur parsing and performance costs.
A dynamically created function cannot close over local variables from the scope that constructed it.

Generator.summary: A Generator is the iterator object produced by a generator function. It combines iterable and iterator behavior, allowing execution to pause at yield and resume later.
Generator.explanation: A Generator is the iterator object produced when a generator function is called. It pauses at each yield, resumes through next(), and also supports throw() and return(); because it implements both iterator and iterable protocols, it can be used with for...of and spread syntax.
Generator.returns: A generator function call returns a new Generator object.

example.title: Creating and consuming a Generator
example.explanation: A generator function call creates a Generator that yields values on demand and can be consumed with iterator operations or for...of.

useCases.title: Lazy sequences
useCases.scenario: Produce sequence values only as consumers request them, avoiding eager creation of the full sequence.

useCases.title: Infinite or expensive data
useCases.scenario: Represent an unbounded or computationally expensive sequence without calculating every value in advance.

useCases.title: Custom iteration
useCases.scenario: Expose custom iteration behavior through for...of, spread syntax, and other iterable consumers.

useCases.title: Cooperative control flow
useCases.scenario: Pause an algorithm and exchange values bidirectionally between the generator and its caller.

interview.question: What is a Generator, and how is it obtained?
interview.answer: A Generator is an object returned by calling a generator function. It conforms to both the iterator and iterable protocols, so it provides iterator control methods and can be consumed by iteration constructs.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from an ordinary function? A generator function suspends and later resumes execution around yield, while an ordinary function runs to completion when called.

interview.question: What does Generator.prototype.next() return?
interview.answer: next() resumes the suspended generator and returns an iterator-result object containing value and done. The yielded expression supplies value while done indicates whether iteration has finished.
interview.followUp: What does passing an argument to next() do? After the first resume, that argument becomes the result of the currently suspended yield expression.

interview.question: How do return() and throw() affect a Generator?
interview.answer: return() finishes the generator as though a return statement were inserted at its current suspended position. This lets generator cleanup run when the body uses try...finally.
interview.followUp: How can an error be injected? throw() resumes the generator by throwing an exception at its suspended position, allowing generator code to catch or propagate it.

keyPoints: Calling a generator function returns an object usable both as an iterator and as an iterable.
The built-in Generator type inherits from Iterator.
A newly created Generator starts suspended before its function body has executed.
The caller controls resumption, exception injection, or completion through next(), throw(), and return().
While a yield produces another item, next() reports that item with done set to false.
Generators are lazy, evaluating each yielded value only when consumption requests it.
gotchas: A Generator is single-use: after it is exhausted, subsequent iteration does not replay the yielded values.
Do not instantiate Generator with new; obtain one by calling a generator function.
Calling a generator function creates the Generator without running its body until next(), iteration, or another control method is used.

globalThis.summary: globalThis is the portable global property for accessing JavaScript's global this value. It works in both window and non-window contexts, although hosts and browsers may implement its identity differently.
globalThis.explanation: globalThis is a standard global property that evaluates to the global this value. It provides one environment-independent way to reach the global object, though a host may technically provide a different value; browsers may expose a Proxy for security reasons.

example.title: Access the global object
example.explanation: The snippet stores a property on the global object and reads it through the portable globalThis reference.

useCases.title: Access environment-wide APIs without choosing window, self, or global.
useCases.scenario: Portable runtime code

useCases.title: Expose or read a property through one consistent global reference.
useCases.scenario: Shared global configuration

useCases.title: Check whether a global API or capability exists across JavaScript hosts.
useCases.scenario: Runtime feature detection

interview.question: What problem does globalThis solve?
interview.answer: globalThis is the standard, portable reference to the global this value. Unlike window or self, it works in both window and non-window contexts.
interview.followUp: What can differ in a browser? globalThis may refer to a Proxy around the actual global object, particularly because of iframe and cross-window security considerations.

interview.question: How does globalThis relate to top-level this?
interview.answer: In a script's global scope, this and globalThis refer to the global this value. In a module's top-level scope, this is undefined, so globalThis is the reliable explicit reference.
interview.followUp: How does direct eval differ? Direct eval inherits the enclosing this, while indirect eval uses globalThis as if evaluated in a separate global script.

interview.question: Is globalThis always the global object?
interview.answer: It is usually the same concept as the global object, and adding properties to it makes them global variables in browsers and Node. However, hosts may provide a different value.
interview.followUp: Do top-level declarations always become globalThis properties? No: top-level let and const declarations do not create properties of the global object.

keyPoints: Its value is the global this object.
It gives code a standardized way to access the global this value.
It works across window and non-window environments.
Code can use it without identifying the current JavaScript environment.
It matches this inside a non-strict function invoked without an object receiver.
In a classic script's global scope, global this is the same value.
gotchas: Do not assume every host makes globalThis identical to its global object.
In browsers, globalThis can be a Proxy rather than the underlying global object.
Creating a top-level let or const binding does not make a same-named globalThis property.

includes.summary: `String.prototype.includes()` performs a case-sensitive substring search and reports whether the requested text occurs in a string. It returns a boolean and accepts an optional starting position.
includes.explanation: Call `includes()` on a string with the text to find, optionally providing the zero-based position where searching should start. It returns a boolean and compares characters case-sensitively; the starting position is converted and constrained to the string’s bounds.

parameters.name: searchString
parameters.description: The string to look for within the receiver. It must not be a regular expression; other values are converted to strings.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: The zero-based position at which to begin searching. It defaults to 0.

includes.returns: A boolean: `true` if the search string occurs at or after the starting position; otherwise `false`.

example.title: Checking whether a string contains text
example.code:
const text = "To be, or not to be, that is the question.";

console.log(text.includes("question")); // true
console.log(text.includes("TO BE")); // false
console.log(text.includes("be", 10)); // false
console.log(text.includes("")); // true
example.explanation: The method performs a case-sensitive substring check and can begin searching at the supplied position.

useCases.title: Check whether user input contains a required token
useCases.scenario: Validate input

useCases.title: Keep strings that contain a specific word or phrase
useCases.scenario: Filter text

useCases.title: Choose a branch based on substring presence
useCases.scenario: Guard conditional logic

useCases.title: Ignore a prefix by starting at a later position
useCases.scenario: Search from an offset

interview.question: What does String.prototype.includes() return?
interview.answer: `String.prototype.includes()` returns a boolean indicating whether a string contains the supplied substring. The comparison is case-sensitive, and an empty search string is considered present.
interview.followUp: What happens when the search argument is a regular expression? It throws a TypeError rather than performing a pattern search.

interview.question: How does the position argument affect the search?
interview.answer: The optional `position` argument specifies where the search begins and defaults to zero. It is converted to an integer-like value and constrained to the string’s valid range.
interview.followUp: Does a position beyond the string length match an empty search string? Yes, because the empty string is found at the effective endpoint.

interview.question: How are non-string search arguments handled?
interview.answer: The method coerces non-regexp search values to strings. If the argument is omitted or is `undefined`, the searched value becomes the string `"undefined"`.
interview.followUp: How can a case-insensitive search be implemented? Convert both the source and search strings to the same case before calling `includes()`.

keyPoints: It checks whether the receiver contains the requested substring using case-sensitive matching.
The result is a boolean: `true` when the substring is found and `false` otherwise.
An optional position lets you skip earlier characters when starting the search.
If no starting position is supplied, searching begins at index zero.
An empty search string returns `true`, including when the source string itself is empty.
Search arguments other than regular expressions are converted to strings before matching.
gotchas: The search value cannot be a regular expression; passing one throws a TypeError.
Omitting the search argument or explicitly passing `undefined` searches for the literal string "undefined".
Different letter casing does not match; normalize both strings first when a case-insensitive check is needed.

indexOf.summary: Array.prototype.indexOf() returns the first index where a value occurs in an array, or -1 when it is absent. It optionally accepts a starting index and uses strict equality for matching.
indexOf.explanation: Call this method with a value to search an array from the beginning, or provide a starting index. It checks elements in ascending order with strict equality, returns the first matching position, and returns -1 when no match exists; sparse-array holes are skipped.

parameters.name: searchElement
parameters.description: The value to locate in the array.

parameters.name: fromIndex
parameters.description: Optional zero-based starting index, converted to an integer. Negative values count from the end.

indexOf.returns: The first index of searchElement in the array; -1 if not found.

example.title: Find an array element's index
example.explanation: This finds the first matching value, reports absence with -1, and can begin searching at a specified index.

useCases.title: Membership with a position
useCases.scenario: Check whether a value occurs while retaining its position when present.

useCases.title: Search from an offset
useCases.scenario: Find a later occurrence by beginning the search after an earlier match.

useCases.title: Handle array-like data
useCases.scenario: Apply the method to objects that expose length and integer-keyed properties.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.indexOf return?
interview.answer: It returns the first index where the searched value occurs, or -1 when no element matches. Matching uses strict equality, equivalent to the === comparison algorithm.
interview.followUp: How would you find NaN? Use Number.isNaN while scanning, or use includes when only a presence check is needed, because indexOf(NaN) always returns -1.

interview.question: How does fromIndex affect the search?
interview.answer: The optional fromIndex is converted to an integer and determines where the search starts. A negative value is counted from the end, while a value beyond the array length prevents searching.
interview.followUp: What happens with a negative fromIndex smaller than -array.length? It is treated as 0, so the complete array is searched.

interview.question: Is indexOf limited to Array instances?
interview.answer: The method is generic: it only requires a this value with a length property and integer-keyed properties. Therefore, it can operate on array-like objects as well as actual arrays.
interview.followUp: Does generic mean it works on every object? No; the object still needs a usable length and indexed properties for meaningful results.

keyPoints: The result identifies the earliest matching position, or signals that the value is absent with -1.
The method accepts the value to locate and an optional starting position.
fromIndex is zero-based and converted to an integer before searching begins.
Negative starting positions are interpreted relative to the array's end.
Values are matched with strict equality rather than coercive equality.
The operation can be borrowed for suitable array-like objects.
gotchas: A search for NaN always fails because strict equality does not consider NaN equal to itself.
It cannot locate a sparse-array hole, because empty slots are not visited.
A starting index at or beyond the array length immediately produces -1.

Intl.summary: `Intl` is the namespace for JavaScript's ECMAScript Internationalization API. Its constructors and utilities provide locale-sensitive comparison, formatting, and other language-aware operations.
Intl.explanation: Intl is a namespace object for the ECMAScript Internationalization API. Its constructors and static utilities support locale-sensitive comparison, number formatting, date and time formatting, and other language-aware operations; it is used through its static members and constructors rather than called or instantiated itself.

parameters.name: locales
parameters.description: Preferred locale identifier, an `Intl.Locale` object, a locale list, or `undefined` to use the default locale.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: An object whose available properties depend on the constructor or function using it.

example.title: Locale-sensitive date and currency formatting
example.explanation: The formatters use the browser's preferred locale to produce localized date and currency strings.

useCases.title: Localized date and time display
useCases.scenario: Render dates and times according to a user's language and regional conventions.

useCases.title: Localized numeric output
useCases.scenario: Format prices, measurements, and quantities using locale-appropriate separators and patterns.

useCases.title: Locale-aware text comparison
useCases.scenario: Compare or sort user-facing text according to language-specific collation rules.

useCases.title: Locale negotiation and locale utilities
useCases.scenario: Inspect or normalize locale preferences before selecting an internationalized UI behavior.

interview.question: What is `Intl` in JavaScript?
interview.answer: `Intl` is a namespace object that groups the ECMAScript Internationalization API. It provides constructors and shared functionality for locale-sensitive tasks such as string comparison, number formatting, and date and time formatting.
interview.followUp: How are requested locales handled? Constructors and language-sensitive methods negotiate the requested locale list against supported locales, using the `localeMatcher` option when applicable.

interview.question: Can `Intl` be called or instantiated directly?
interview.answer: `Intl` itself is not constructible or callable, and its members are static. Individual API objects, such as `Intl.NumberFormat`, are created through their own constructors.
interview.followUp: What happens when no locale is supplied? The implementation uses its default locale, while an explicitly supplied locale or locale list expresses the preferred language or region.

interview.question: What are the common `locales` and `options` arguments?
interview.answer: The `locales` argument identifies the preferred locale for an operation. It can be omitted, supplied as one locale identifier or `Intl.Locale` object, or supplied as a list of locales; the implementation selects the closest supported locale.
interview.followUp: What does `options` do? It is an object whose properties vary by constructor or function and can control formatting or locale negotiation behavior.

keyPoints: The namespace covers multiple internationalization features rather than one formatting operation.
Use its exposed static members directly; the namespace does not have instance methods.
Locale input selects the linguistic and regional conventions for an operation.
Locale negotiation chooses the best supported match instead of requiring every requested locale to be available.
A single locale may be represented by a BCP 47-style identifier or an `Intl.Locale` instance.
Multiple preferences can be supplied so the runtime can try fallback locales.
gotchas: Do not use `new Intl()`; the namespace itself cannot be constructed.
Calling `Intl()` or applying `new` to `Intl` throws instead of performing an operation.

isFinite.summary: `Number.isFinite()` checks whether a value is a finite JavaScript number. It returns `false` for non-numbers, `NaN`, and positive or negative infinity.
isFinite.explanation: Call `Number.isFinite(value)` to test whether `value` is both a number and finite. Unlike the global `isFinite()` function, it does not convert non-number inputs before testing, so non-numbers return `false`.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to be tested for finiteness.

isFinite.returns: A Boolean: `true` for a finite number and `false` otherwise.

example.title: Filtering finite numeric values
example.explanation: Only the numeric value 42 passes; strings and other non-finite or non-number values return false.

useCases.title: Strict numeric validation
useCases.scenario: Validate numeric input before arithmetic or calculations.

useCases.title: Filtering datasets
useCases.scenario: Keep only finite numeric elements when processing mixed data.

useCases.title: Guarding calculations
useCases.scenario: Reject sentinel values such as `NaN` and infinities in computation pipelines.

interview.question: What does `Number.isFinite()` test?
interview.answer: `Number.isFinite(value)` returns `true` only when `value` has the number type and is not `NaN`, positive `Infinity`, or negative `Infinity`. It returns `false` for every other value.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from global `isFinite()`? The global function converts non-number arguments first, while `Number.isFinite()` does not.

interview.question: What are representative inputs and outputs?
interview.answer: The method accepts one value to test and returns a Boolean. Finite numeric values such as `0` and `2e64` produce `true`; `NaN` and either infinity produce `false`.
interview.followUp: What happens for a string such as `"0"`? `Number.isFinite("0")` is `false` because the argument is not a number.

interview.question: When is `Number.isFinite()` preferable to global `isFinite()`?
interview.answer: Use it when input must already be a JavaScript number and must also be usable as a finite numeric value. It combines type strictness with rejection of `NaN` and both infinities.
interview.followUp: Would it validate an integer? No; finite fractional values also pass, so use an integer-specific check when integerness is required.

keyPoints: It is a static method on `Number`, called as `Number.isFinite(value)` rather than as a method on an individual number.
A successful result requires both numeric type and finiteness; `NaN` and either sign of infinity fail.
Its complete call signature takes one argument named `value`.
The argument can be any value; the method determines whether that value qualifies as a finite number.
The return type is Boolean, with `true` reserved for finite numbers.
gotchas: Do not substitute the global `isFinite()` when you need strict numeric validation: that function coerces its argument first.
Numeric-looking strings and values such as `null` are rejected rather than converted.

Iterator.summary: Iterator is the abstract base class for JavaScript iterator objects. Subclass it to implement next(), then use its iterable behavior and lazy helper methods to process sequences.
Iterator.explanation: Iterator is an abstract base class for iterator objects. A subclass implements next() to produce iterator-result objects, while the class supplies iterable behavior and helper methods such as take(), map(), filter(), and toArray(); Iterator.from() can adapt an existing iterator or iterable.

interview.question: What is the Iterator class and what must a subclass provide?
interview.answer: Iterator is the base class for iterator objects. A subclass must implement next(), which returns an iterator result; Iterator also makes instances iterable by returning themselves from [Symbol.iterator]().
interview.followUp: How would you adapt a library iterator? Use Iterator.from(), which returns an existing Iterator directly or wraps a non-Iterator iterator.

interview.question: Can you instantiate Iterator directly?
interview.answer: The constructor is intended as a superclass constructor rather than a directly usable class. Calling it without new throws, and constructing Iterator itself is not supported as a standalone operation.
interview.followUp: What does Iterator.from() do for an iterable? It calls the iterable's [Symbol.iterator]() method and adapts the resulting iterator when necessary.

interview.question: Why use Iterator helper methods instead of array methods?
interview.answer: Iterator helpers are lazy iterator operations: they produce values only when the resulting helper's next() is requested. This allows transformations and limits to avoid eagerly creating an array.
interview.followUp: What happens when a helper reaches the underlying iterator's end? The helper also completes and returns an iterator result with done set to true.

keyPoints: The class is the common superclass for JavaScript's built-in iterator types.
Iterator instances follow the iterator protocol by implementing next() and returning result objects.
An Iterator is also iterable, so for...of and spread can consume it directly.
The class includes helpers for transforming, limiting, testing, and collecting iterator output.
gotchas: Iterator is abstract and cannot be instantiated directly; create a subclass or use Iterator.from().
Calling Iterator() without new throws a TypeError.
Iterator objects are generally single-use: consuming one advances its state and does not reset it.

parameters.name: separator
