parameters.description: An iterable, such as an Array, whose elements may be promises, thenables, or non-promise values.

Promise.allSettled.returns: A Promise that fulfills with an array of outcome objects after all inputs settle. An empty iterable yields an already-fulfilled promise; a non-empty iterable with no pending promises fulfills asynchronously.

example.title: Inspect every settled result
example.explanation: Runs independent requests together, then handles each outcome by checking its discriminating status field.

useCases.title: Batch independent tasks
useCases.scenario: Run independent API requests or background operations while retaining both successful and failed outcomes.

useCases.title: Partial-success processing
useCases.scenario: Collect per-item results when some operations may fail without preventing the rest from completing.

useCases.title: Outcome auditing
useCases.scenario: Inspect every operation after a batch finishes for logging, metrics, or user-facing status reporting.

interview.question: What does Promise.allSettled() return?
interview.answer: It returns one promise that fulfills after every input has settled, whether the individual inputs fulfilled or rejected. Its result is an array ordered like the input, and each item reports status plus either value or reason.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from Promise.all()? Promise.all() rejects as soon as an input rejects, whereas allSettled() waits for every input and reports all outcomes.

interview.question: What kinds of values can the iterable contain?
interview.answer: The iterable can contain promises, thenables, or ordinary values. Values are awaited through promise resolution, while non-thenables become fulfilled outcomes with their values.
interview.followUp: What happens for an empty iterable? The returned promise is already fulfilled with an empty array.

interview.question: How are fulfillment and rejection represented?
interview.answer: A fulfilled record has status set to "fulfilled" and a value property. A rejected record has status set to "rejected" and a reason property, so status should be checked before reading the corresponding field.
interview.followUp: Does completion order affect the result order? No; records remain in the order of the original iterable.

keyPoints: It is a static method on Promise and accepts an iterable rather than requiring an array.
The aggregate promise waits for every input to finish, including rejected inputs.
The fulfillment value is an array of outcome records, one corresponding to each input.
Result positions follow input order, not the order in which asynchronous operations finish.
Each outcome's status discriminates whether the operation succeeded or failed.
The value field exists for fulfilled outcomes, while rejected outcomes use reason instead.
gotchas: Even already-settled non-empty input produces its fulfillment asynchronously, so do not rely on immediate callback execution.

Promise.any.summary: Promise.any() returns a promise fulfilled by the first input that fulfills. It rejects with AggregateError when every input rejects, including an empty iterable.
Promise.any.explanation: Promise.any() converts the supplied iterable's values to promises and returns a promise that succeeds as soon as one input succeeds. It ignores earlier rejections, but if every input rejects—or the iterable is empty—it rejects with an AggregateError whose errors array contains the rejection reasons in input order.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: An iterable, such as an Array, containing promise-like values, promises, or ordinary values.

Promise.any.returns: A Promise that fulfills with the first fulfillment value, or rejects with an AggregateError when all supplied values reject or the iterable is empty.

example.title: Use the first successful promise
example.explanation: The rejection does not win: the returned promise fulfills with the value from the first input promise that fulfills.

useCases.title: Fallback requests
useCases.scenario: Several equivalent services or mirrors can be queried concurrently; use the first successful response.

useCases.title: Alternative algorithms
useCases.scenario: Multiple independent strategies can attempt the same operation, where failures are acceptable until one succeeds.

useCases.title: Resilient provider selection
useCases.scenario: A group of optional providers can be raced for availability while preserving all failure reasons if none works.

interview.question: When does Promise.any() fulfill?
interview.answer: It fulfills with the value of the first input promise to fulfill. Rejections do not settle the result, so an earlier rejection is ignored if another input later succeeds.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from Promise.race()? Promise.race() settles on the first fulfillment or rejection, whereas Promise.any() waits through rejections until a fulfillment occurs.

interview.question: What happens when all inputs reject?
interview.answer: It rejects with an AggregateError when every input rejects, including when the iterable is empty. The error's errors property contains the individual rejection reasons.
interview.followUp: How should failure details be inspected? Catch the error and iterate over error.errors, rather than treating the AggregateError itself as the only cause.

interview.question: What can be passed to Promise.any()?
interview.answer: The argument is an iterable, such as an array, whose values are awaited; thenables are resolved and non-thenables are used as-is. The returned promise settles asynchronously when rejection or fulfillment is determined.
interview.followUp: What ordering applies to collected failures? AggregateError.errors preserves the iterable's input order regardless of completion timing.

keyPoints: It accepts an iterable and produces one promise representing the first successful outcome.
The result carries the fulfillment value from whichever input fulfills first.
No successful input is required for rejection; an empty iterable also rejects.
Inputs need not be native promises: thenables are assimilated and ordinary values pass through.
After the first fulfillment, the result is settled without waiting for remaining operations.
All-failure handling exposes the individual causes through AggregateError.errors.
gotchas: AggregateError.errors follows input order, not the order in which failures happen.
Even already-settled inputs produce an asynchronous rejection when none fulfills.
Calling Promise.any() attaches handling to the inputs immediately.

Promise.race.summary: Promise.race() returns a promise whose outcome follows the first item in an iterable to settle, whether fulfillment or rejection. It always settles asynchronously and remains pending when given an empty iterable.
Promise.race.explanation: Promise.race() converts each item in an iterable into a promise and returns a new promise whose outcome follows whichever item settles first. The outcome may be fulfillment or rejection, and settlement is always asynchronous—even for an empty iterable or an iterable containing only already-settled values.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: An iterable, such as an Array, containing promises, thenables, or other values to race.

Promise.race.returns: A Promise that asynchronously settles with the eventual state of the first item in the iterable to settle; it fulfills with that item's value or rejects with its reason.

example.title: Race a request against a timeout
example.explanation: The first operation to settle determines whether the race fulfills or rejects.

useCases.title: Timeout asynchronous work
useCases.scenario: Use a task together with a rejecting delay to enforce a maximum response time.

useCases.title: Choose the fastest result
useCases.scenario: Start equivalent asynchronous operations and accept whichever responds first.

useCases.title: Race heterogeneous inputs
useCases.scenario: Select among values or promises where the earliest settled candidate should determine the outcome.

interview.question: What does Promise.race() return?
interview.answer: It returns a promise that follows the first promise or value in the iterable to settle. A fulfillment produces fulfillment with that value, while a rejection produces rejection with its reason.
interview.followUp: What happens with an empty iterable? The returned promise remains pending forever, so neither fulfillment nor rejection occurs.

interview.question: What kinds of values can the iterable contain?
interview.answer: The method accepts an iterable, such as an array, whose entries can be promises, thenables, or ordinary values. Thenables are resolved, while non-thenables are used as values.
interview.followUp: How can an ordinary value win? If it appears before an already-settled promise or other non-pending winner in iteration order, it can determine the result.

interview.question: Is Promise.race() ever synchronous?
interview.answer: Promise.race() always settles asynchronously. This remains true even when the iterable is non-empty and contains no pending promises, or when the iterable is empty.
interview.followUp: Why does the empty case differ from the other cases? It stays pending forever because there is no item capable of settling the race.

keyPoints: It is a static Promise method that consumes an iterable and creates one result promise.
The first settlement determines both the result state and its value or rejection reason.
Entries need not already be native promises: thenables are assimilated and ordinary values pass through.
Already-settled promises and non-promise values can win according to their position in the iterable.
It belongs to the standard group of Promise concurrency combinators.
Calling the method attaches handlers to the participating promises immediately.
gotchas: An empty iterable never produces a settled result, so the returned promise stays pending indefinitely.
Already-settled inputs do not make the result synchronous; handlers run asynchronously.
Later failures do not change the result and are treated as handled by the combinator.

Promise.reject.summary: Promise.reject() creates and returns a new promise that is already rejected with the supplied reason. It is useful for producing rejection branches or adapting a value into a rejected promise.
Promise.reject.explanation: Promise.reject(reason) creates an already-rejected promise whose rejection reason is the supplied value. It always creates a new Promise, can be used with Promise subclasses, and is equivalent in effect to constructing a promise whose executor calls reject(reason).

parameters.name: reason
parameters.description: Reason why this Promise rejected.

Promise.reject.returns: A Promise that is rejected with the given reason.

example.title: Reject and handle a promise
example.code:
Promise.reject(new Error("Request failed"))
  .catch((error) => console.error(error.message));
example.explanation: Creates an immediately rejected promise and handles its reason with catch().

useCases.title: Signal an asynchronous failure
useCases.scenario: Return a rejected promise from a function when validation or preconditions fail.

useCases.title: Test rejection handling
useCases.scenario: Create predictable failure inputs for promise-chain or async-handler tests.

useCases.title: Normalize an error path
useCases.scenario: Convert a synchronous error value into a rejected promise for a uniform async API.

keyPoints: Use the static method to create a rejected promise carrying any chosen reason.
It provides a concise alternative to constructing a promise and calling its reject callback.
The method can be called with a compatible constructor, not only the built-in Promise constructor.
A custom constructor must accept an executor function with resolve and reject callbacks.
Calling it never returns the original promise supplied as the reason.
gotchas: The supplied value is always wrapped in a new promise, even when it is already a promise.
Prefer an Error object as the reason when you want useful debugging information and selective error handling.

Promise.resolve.summary: Promise.resolve(value) converts a value, promise, or thenable into a Promise. It reuses eligible existing promises, assimilates thenables, and fulfills with ordinary values.
Promise.resolve.explanation: Promise.resolve(value) produces a promise associated with value. Existing native Promise instances may be returned unchanged; thenables are assimilated by calling then, while ordinary values become fulfillment values, and nested promise-like layers are flattened.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to resolve; it may be an ordinary value, a Promise, or a thenable.

Promise.resolve.returns: A Promise resolved with the supplied value, or the supplied promise when it can be reused. The resulting promise may be fulfilled, rejected, or pending while following another promise-like object.

example.title: Assimilate a thenable
example.explanation: A thenable is assimilated, so the returned promise adopts the value supplied to its then method.

useCases.title: Normalize mixed inputs
useCases.scenario: An API accepts either synchronous values or promises and should expose one consistent promise-based result.

useCases.title: Adopt a thenable
useCases.scenario: Code interoperates with a promise-like object supplied by another library or implementation.

useCases.title: Create a fulfilled promise
useCases.scenario: A function needs to return an immediately fulfilled promise without manually invoking the Promise constructor.

useCases.title: Flatten promise layers
useCases.scenario: Promise-like results may be nested through multiple asynchronous layers and need one consumable promise.

interview.question: What does Promise.resolve do?
interview.answer: It converts a value into a promise. A native promise can be returned directly, a thenable is assimilated by invoking its then method, and an ordinary value produces a fulfilled promise.
interview.followUp: What happens with nested promise-like values? Their layers are flattened, so the resulting promise follows the eventual non-thenable outcome.

interview.question: What are its parameter and return value?
interview.answer: The argument is the value to resolve and may be an ordinary value, a Promise, or a thenable. The method returns a Promise resolved with that argument or the passed promise when identity-preserving conditions apply.
interview.followUp: Can a resolved promise be rejected? Yes: resolution may make it follow a rejected promise or thenable, so resolved and fulfilled are different concepts.

interview.question: How does Promise.resolve handle thenables?
interview.answer: A thenable is an object with a then method. Promise.resolve calls that method with resolving callbacks, allowing the returned promise to adopt the thenable's eventual state.
interview.followUp: Why assimilate thenables? It lets native promises interoperate with promise-like objects from other implementations or libraries.

keyPoints: It is a static method on Promise that normalizes an input into promise-based control flow.
Non-thenable inputs become the fulfillment value of the returned promise.
Promise-like nesting is collapsed so consumers handle one promise layer rather than recursively unwrapping it.
An eligible existing promise is reused instead of being wrapped in another promise.
Thenable assimilation invokes its then method with resolving functions supplied by the implementation.
gotchas: “Resolved” does not necessarily mean fulfilled: the returned promise can remain pending or can be rejected while following another promise or thenable.
Passing an existing promise can preserve its identity rather than creating a wrapper; this behavior is specific to the applicable Promise constructor and instance.
Do not treat the method name as an immediate fulfillment operation; resolution establishes what outcome the returned promise will follow.

Promise.withResolvers.summary: Promise.withResolvers() returns a new promise together with the resolve and reject functions that control it. This makes it convenient to settle a promise from code outside its constructor executor.
Promise.withResolvers.explanation: Promise.withResolvers() creates a promise together with the resolve and reject functions associated with it. Because those functions are returned in the same scope as the promise, external code such as an event listener can settle it later.
Promise.withResolvers.returns: A plain object containing promise, resolve, and reject properties.

example.title: Resolve a promise from an event listener
example.explanation: The promise is controlled by an event listener outside the constructor executor.

useCases.title: Event-driven completion
useCases.scenario: An event listener must complete an asynchronous operation later.

useCases.title: Callback-to-promise coordination
useCases.scenario: External callback code needs to report success or failure through one promise.

useCases.title: Promise subclassing
useCases.scenario: A compatible Promise subclass should preserve its own promise type.

interview.question: What does Promise.withResolvers() return?
interview.answer: It returns a plain object with three properties: promise, resolve, and reject. The promise is new, while the two functions settle that promise.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from constructing a promise manually? The functions are exposed in the surrounding scope rather than being captured from inside the executor.

interview.question: When would you use Promise.withResolvers()?
interview.answer: It is useful when an event listener or another external callback must resolve or reject a promise. The callback can retain the returned functions and settle the promise when the event occurs.
interview.followUp: What problem does this avoid? It avoids having to place the external event logic inside the Promise constructor's executor.

interview.question: Does Promise.withResolvers() support subclassing?
interview.answer: The method is generic and supports Promise subclasses. Calling it with a compatible subclass produces a promise of that subclass type.
interview.followUp: What compatibility requirement applies? The subclass constructor must accept a single executor function that receives resolve and reject callbacks.

keyPoints: The static method packages a newly created promise with its settlement functions.
Its result is an ordinary object whose named properties are promise, resolve, and reject.
The resolve property settles the associated promise successfully.
The reject property settles the associated promise unsuccessfully.
The generic operation can be applied to compatible Promise-like constructors, not only the built-in Promise constructor.
gotchas: The returned functions remain available outside the promise executor, so external code can settle the promise later.
When used with a Promise subclass, that subclass must accept one executor function with resolve and reject callbacks.

Proxy.summary: The Proxy() constructor creates a proxy that wraps a target object and can intercept selected fundamental operations. A handler supplies trap functions for customizing those operations.
Proxy.explanation: A Proxy wraps a target object and uses handler trap functions to intercept selected fundamental operations, such as property reads and writes. Each trap can customize the operation or delegate to the corresponding Reflect method. The target may be an object, array, function, or another proxy.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The object to wrap. It may be an array, function, or another proxy.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: An object whose function-valued properties define the proxy's custom behavior.

Proxy.returns: A new Proxy object that wraps target and applies the behavior defined by handler.

example.title: Log property access
example.explanation: The proxy logs property reads, then delegates the actual lookup to Reflect.get.

useCases.title: Observe operations
useCases.scenario: Record reads or writes for debugging, auditing, or metrics.

useCases.title: Validate data
useCases.scenario: Reject invalid assignments or enforce object invariants at runtime.

useCases.title: Customize access
useCases.scenario: Present computed, normalized, or virtual properties through an object-like interface.

useCases.title: Adapt an interface
useCases.scenario: Hide or transform selected values while exposing a compatible object API.

keyPoints: Use the Proxy constructor to create an object that stands in for another object.
Code can generally use the proxy where it would use the original target.
The target is the object being wrapped and can be an array, function, or another proxy.
The handler contains trap methods that define which operations are intercepted.
Define only the traps needed for behaviors such as logging, validation, or transformation.
Typical uses include observing access, validating assignments, and normalizing or sanitizing values.
gotchas: Always use new Proxy(...); calling Proxy(...) without new throws a TypeError.
An empty handler does not add custom behavior; it mostly mirrors the target.

queueMicrotask.sourceTitle: Window: queueMicrotask () method - Web APIs | MDN
queueMicrotask.summary: queueMicrotask() schedules a function as a microtask. The function runs after the current task completes, before control returns to the event loop.
queueMicrotask.explanation: Calling queueMicrotask(callback) places callback in the microtask queue. After the current task finishes and the JavaScript stack is empty, the runtime drains pending microtasks before yielding back to the event loop; callbacks added while draining run in that same draining phase.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: A function invoked when the runtime determines that it is safe to execute the callback.

example.title: Schedule work before the next task
example.explanation: The scheduled callback runs after the current synchronous code finishes, so the output is ["task", "after scheduling", "microtask"].

useCases.title: Consistent deferred notifications
useCases.scenario: A library needs to normalize synchronous and asynchronous completion so observers are notified consistently after the current operation.

useCases.title: Pre-render cleanup
useCases.scenario: A framework or component needs final cleanup or work immediately before rendering.

useCases.title: Ordered asynchronous follow-up
useCases.scenario: Code must preserve the order of short asynchronous follow-up operations without waiting for a later task.

interview.question: When does a queued microtask execute?
interview.answer: queueMicrotask(callback) schedules callback for the microtask queue. It runs after the current task completes and before control returns to the event loop.
interview.followUp: How does it compare with setTimeout(..., 0)? setTimeout schedules a later task, while a queued microtask is drained before the next task begins.

interview.question: What are queueMicrotask()'s parameter and return value?
interview.answer: The function takes one callback parameter, which is invoked when the runtime determines it is safe to run the code. The method itself returns undefined.
interview.followUp: What happens if the callback queues another microtask? The newly queued microtask runs before the next task because microtask processing continues until the queue is empty.

interview.question: When is queueMicrotask() useful?
interview.answer: Microtasks provide asynchronous execution with deterministic ordering. They are useful when code must run after the current operation but before the browser regains control, including library cleanup or just-before-rendering work.
interview.followUp: Why can recursive scheduling be harmful? Since newly added microtasks are processed before the next task, continuous scheduling can postpone tasks and rendering.

keyPoints: queueMicrotask() schedules a callback to run before the browser regains control.
Its callback is a function supplied by the caller.
The callback runs after pending task work and before yielding to the event loop.
Microtasks let code run asynchronously while preserving scheduling order.
Libraries and frameworks can use it for final cleanup or work immediately before rendering.
Microtasks queued from another microtask run before the next task.
gotchas: Microtasks may run more often than once per event-loop iteration, so avoid using them for unbounded or expensive work.
A microtask that continually queues more microtasks can delay subsequent tasks.
The callback receives no arguments, and its return value is not used by queueMicrotask().

Reflect.summary: Reflect is a namespace object containing static methods that invoke interceptable JavaScript object operations. It is primarily used to forward default behavior from Proxy traps.
Reflect.explanation: Reflect is a namespace object whose static methods invoke JavaScript object internal methods, such as property access, assignment, construction, and function calls. It is especially useful inside Proxy traps when a trap should add behavior while preserving the operation's normal semantics.
Reflect.returns: Each static method returns the result specified by the corresponding operation; the exact return value depends on the method.

example.title: Forward Proxy Operations with Reflect
example.explanation: The proxy logs reads while Reflect forwards the intercepted operations using JavaScript's default object behavior.

useCases.title: Forward Proxy traps
useCases.scenario: A Proxy trap needs to log, validate, or transform an operation while retaining ordinary JavaScript behavior.

useCases.title: Explicit reflective operations
useCases.scenario: Code needs to invoke property, construction, or function-call semantics explicitly rather than using syntax.

useCases.title: Implement meta-programming utilities
useCases.scenario: Meta-programming code needs operations that match Proxy handler trap semantics.

interview.question: What is Reflect?
interview.answer: Reflect is a built-in namespace object containing static methods that correspond to interceptable object internal methods. It is not a constructor or callable function.
interview.followUp: Why is it commonly used in Proxy traps? It provides the default forwarding operation, allowing the trap to add behavior without manually reproducing ordinary semantics.

interview.question: How do Reflect and Proxy work together?
interview.answer: A Proxy trap intercepts an operation, while the matching Reflect method performs the corresponding default internal operation. For example, a get trap can call Reflect.get with the target, property, and receiver.
interview.followUp: Can Reflect bypass another proxy? No. The operation still goes through object internal methods, so a proxy target remains proxied.

interview.question: What are the main uses of Reflect?
interview.answer: Reflect methods use function-style forms of operations such as property lookup, assignment, construction, and invocation. This makes those operations explicit and useful for forwarding from traps.
interview.followUp: What recursion risk exists? If a trap calls the corresponding Reflect method with the proxy as the target, the same trap can be triggered again indefinitely.

keyPoints: Reflect exposes static functions for explicitly invoking internal object operations.
Its method names correspond to Proxy handler trap operations.
Methods are accessed directly on Reflect rather than through instances.
Use Reflect in a trap when custom logic should preserve the operation's default behavior.
Proxy traps customize fundamental operations represented by object internal methods.
Each Reflect operation invokes the matching internal object method.
gotchas: Reflect cannot be called with new and is not callable as a function; use its static methods directly.

RegExp.summary: RegExp represents a pattern for matching text. Create it with literal syntax or the constructor, then use it with RegExp and String matching methods.
RegExp.explanation: RegExp represents a pattern used to search text. Create one with slash notation or the constructor; the constructor accepts a pattern and optional flags, and instances provide matching methods such as test() and exec().
RegExp.syntax:
new RegExp(pattern)
new RegExp(pattern, flags)
RegExp(pattern)
RegExp(pattern, flags)

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: The pattern to compile, supplied as a string or a RegExp object.

parameters.name: flags
parameters.description: Optional flags that modify interpretation or interaction with input text.

RegExp.returns: A RegExp object representing the compiled pattern; in the special RegExp(pattern) case, the supplied RegExp may be returned directly.

example.title: Create and use a regular expression
example.code:
const word = new RegExp("cat", "gi");

console.log(word.test("A CAT sleeps.")); // true
console.log(word.flags); // "gi"
console.log(word.source); // "cat"
example.explanation: Creates a case-insensitive, global regular expression and tests whether the input contains a matching word.

useCases.title: Pattern validation
useCases.scenario: Validate or detect text patterns such as identifiers, tokens, or simple formats.

useCases.title: Text extraction
useCases.scenario: Extract matching portions and capture groups from input strings.

useCases.title: String processing
useCases.scenario: Perform replacements, searches, splitting, or iteration over matches.

interview.question: How can a JavaScript RegExp be created?
interview.answer: RegExp objects describe text-matching patterns. They can be created with a literal such as /ab+c/g or with new RegExp(pattern, flags), which is useful when the pattern is assembled dynamically.
interview.followUp: When is the constructor preferable to a literal? Use it when the pattern or flags come from runtime values; remember that string escaping rules apply before the regular-expression parser sees the pattern.

interview.question: What are the RegExp constructor parameters?
interview.answer: The first constructor argument is the pattern, which may be a string or another RegExp object. The optional second argument is a string containing flags that affect matching behavior.
interview.followUp: What happens when a RegExp pattern is passed without new? If the pattern is already a RegExp and flags are undefined, the existing pattern may be returned directly; otherwise a new RegExp object is created.

interview.question: How is a RegExp used for matching text?
interview.answer: A regular expression can be used with instance methods such as test() to check for a match or exec() to obtain match information. It also interoperates with String methods including match(), replace(), search(), and split().
interview.followUp: Why can repeated test() calls differ for /x/g? Global matching advances lastIndex after successful matches, so later calls resume from the stored position.

keyPoints: RegExp packages a text pattern that can be applied to strings.
Use slash syntax for fixed patterns or the constructor when values must be built at runtime.
A literal places the pattern between slashes and appends any needed flags after the closing slash.
The constructor accepts either textual pattern data or an existing regular expression as its first argument.
Its second argument is an optional flags string controlling how the expression behaves.
Supplying a regex and flags constructs a regex using the source of the supplied expression and the requested flags.
gotchas: When a RegExp is supplied as the pattern and flags are also supplied, the new object uses the original source with the explicitly provided flags.

repeat.summary: String.prototype.repeat() returns a new string containing the receiver repeated a specified number of times. The count is converted to an integer and invalid or excessive counts throw RangeError.
repeat.explanation: String.prototype.repeat() returns a new string made by concatenating the receiver a specified number of times. The count is converted to an integer; zero produces an empty string, while invalid or overly large counts throw a RangeError.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: An integer between 0 and Infinity indicating how many times to repeat the string.

repeat.returns: A new string containing the specified number of copies of the given string.

example.title: Create a repeated separator
example.explanation: Creates a five-character separator by concatenating five copies of the same string.

useCases.title: Formatting text
useCases.scenario: Generate a visual divider or indentation by repeating a character or short string.

useCases.title: Constructing strings
useCases.scenario: Create a repeated token sequence when building output or test fixtures.

useCases.title: Aligning output
useCases.scenario: Produce padding based on a calculated width.

interview.question: What does String.prototype.repeat() return?
interview.answer: It returns a new string containing the receiver repeated count times. A count of zero returns an empty string.
interview.followUp: What happens with a fractional count? It is converted to an integer, so 3.5 behaves like 3.

interview.question: When does repeat() throw?
interview.answer: The count must be non-negative and finite, and the resulting string must fit within the maximum string length. Otherwise, the method throws RangeError.
interview.followUp: Does Infinity mean unlimited repetition? No. Infinity is invalid and results in RangeError.

interview.question: Can repeat() be called on a non-String object?
interview.answer: repeat() is generic: it can be borrowed by an object whose this value can be converted to a string. For example, an object with toString() returning "abc" can use String.prototype.repeat.call(object, 2).
interview.followUp: What must a borrowed receiver provide? It must be coercible to a string; the method does not require a String instance.

keyPoints: It creates and returns a separate string rather than modifying the original string.
Each copy is joined directly after the previous one, with no separator inserted.
The count argument controls how many copies are produced and may be zero.
The return value is always a string representing the repeated content.
The method can be borrowed when the receiver can be converted to a string.
gotchas: A negative count, Infinity, or a result too large for the implementation's maximum string length causes a RangeError.
Fractional counts are truncated through integer conversion, so 3.5 repeats the string three times.

replace.summary: String.prototype.replace() returns a new string with matching text replaced. String patterns replace only the first occurrence; use a global regular expression or replaceAll() for all occurrences.
replace.explanation: Call replace() on a string with a string or pattern to search and a string or callback to generate replacement text. It returns a new string, leaving the original unchanged; a string pattern affects only its first occurrence, while a regular expression with the g flag can replace every match.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: The search value: a string, a regular expression, or an object providing Symbol.replace; values without that method are converted to strings.

parameters.name: replacement
parameters.description: Replacement text, or a function called for each match whose return value supplies the replacement text.

replace.returns: A new string with one, some, or all matches of the pattern replaced by the specified replacement.

example.title: Reorder captured date parts
example.explanation: A regular expression captures the date parts, and replacement tokens insert them in month/day/year order.

useCases.title: Single literal substitution
useCases.scenario: Replace a known literal prefix or token once.

useCases.title: Pattern-based rewriting
useCases.scenario: Transform every match with regular expressions and capture groups.

useCases.title: Computed replacements
useCases.scenario: Generate replacement text from match data.

interview.question: What does String.prototype.replace() return and accept?
interview.answer: replace(pattern, replacement) returns a new string with matching text substituted. The pattern may be a string or an object implementing Symbol.replace, and the replacement may be a string or function.
interview.followUp: How can every occurrence of a literal substring be replaced? Use replaceAll(), or use a regular expression with the global g flag.

interview.question: How does replacement count differ for string and RegExp patterns?
interview.answer: A string pattern is searched only once, so only its first occurrence is replaced. A global regular expression can match multiple occurrences.
interview.followUp: What happens if the original string is not assigned the result? The source remains unchanged, because strings and this method do not mutate it.

interview.question: When should the replacement argument be a function?
interview.answer: A replacement function is called for each match, and its return value becomes that match's replacement text. This is useful when replacement content depends on the matched text or captures.
interview.followUp: How can captured groups be used? Define capturing groups in the regular expression and read the corresponding callback arguments, then construct the returned replacement.

The second argument may compute replacement text independently for each match.

Do not expect replace() to mutate the source string; assign the returned value if the updated text must be retained.
A replacement callback runs once per match, so its arguments and returned text determine each substitution.

interview.question: How does replaceAll differ from replace?
interview.answer: replaceAll returns a new string with every match of the pattern replaced. Unlike replace with a string pattern, it does not stop after the first occurrence.
interview.followUp: What happens with a non-global RegExp? It throws a TypeError because replaceAll requires the g flag.

interview.question: What types of arguments does replaceAll accept?
interview.answer: The pattern may be a string or an object providing Symbol.replace, commonly a RegExp. The replacement may be a string or a function invoked for each match.
interview.followUp: Why can a custom object participate? replaceAll can call that object's Symbol.replace method with the target string and replacement.

interview.question: What does replaceAll return, and does it mutate the source?
interview.answer: The method leaves the original string unchanged and returns the resulting replacement string. A string pattern is converted as needed, while a regular expression must be global.
interview.followUp: When is replace preferable? Use replace when only one replacement is intended or when a non-global regular expression is appropriate.

useCases.scenario: Create a reversed result without changing source data.

useCases.title: Handle array-like values
useCases.scenario: Reverse array-like objects that expose length and integer-keyed properties.

The first and last elements exchange positions, continuing inward.
The return value is the original array after mutation.
Empty slots are preserved when an array is reversed.
The method can operate on array-like objects with a length and integer-keyed properties.

useCases.title: Visited-object tracking
useCases.scenario: Track object references that have been visited without duplicating the same reference.

interview.question: What problem does Set solve, and what order does it preserve?
interview.answer: Set stores unique values of any type, including primitives and object references. A value can occur only once, and iteration follows successful insertion order.
interview.followUp: How are object values compared? They use object identity, so only the same object reference is recognized as the existing value.

interview.question: How does Set determine whether two values are the same?
interview.answer: Set equality uses SameValueZero. Consequently, NaN is considered equal to NaN, while object values are compared by reference.
interview.followUp: What happens with duplicate objects? Distinct object literals remain distinct entries even when their properties are equal.

interview.question: How is a Set initialized from existing data?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts an optional iterable, such as an array, and adds its elements to the new Set. If the argument is omitted, null, or undefined, the Set starts empty.
interview.followUp: How can a Set be converted to an array? Spread the Set into an array, which consumes its insertion-order iterator.

keyPoints: Set can contain primitives and object references, while preventing duplicate entries.
Adding an already-present value does not create another entry.
Iteration exposes values in the order in which successful add() calls first inserted them.
Set is a value collection rather than a key-value structure like Map.
Use add(value) to insert conditionally; the method preserves uniqueness.
Use has(value) for a boolean membership test.
entries() yields two-item arrays whose key and value are both the Set value.
gotchas: Membership uses SameValueZero: NaN matches NaN, and 0 and -0 are treated as equal.
Objects are compared by reference, so two separately created objects with identical contents are different Set values.
Calling Set without new throws a TypeError; use new Set() or new Set(iterable).

interview.question: What is SharedArrayBuffer used for?
interview.answer: SharedArrayBuffer is a raw binary memory buffer whose underlying storage can be accessed by multiple agents. Unlike ArrayBuffer, it is shared rather than transferred between execution contexts.
interview.followUp: How is it passed to another worker? Use postMessage with structured cloning; the shared underlying memory remains accessible to both agents.

interview.question: How do you access data in a SharedArrayBuffer?
interview.answer: Create it with new SharedArrayBuffer(length), then expose its bytes through a typed-array view such as Int32Array. The buffer itself is not directly read or written.
interview.followUp: How would you make concurrent integer updates safe? Use Atomics methods on an appropriate integer typed-array view.

interview.question: How can a SharedArrayBuffer be resized?
interview.answer: Pass maxByteLength in the constructor options to make the buffer growable. A growable buffer can increase in size with grow(), but SharedArrayBuffer instances cannot be shrunk.
interview.followUp: What should determine maxByteLength? Set it to the smallest practical maximum, because unnecessarily large limits increase out-of-memory risk.

keyPoints: It supplies a low-level byte storage area rather than an array of JavaScript elements.
ArrayBuffer and SharedArrayBuffer are buffer types; typed arrays provide views for interpreting their bytes.
Structured cloning through postMessage lets agents such as a page and worker access shared storage.
Providing a maximum byte length at construction enables later growth.
gotchas: Browser code needs a secure, cross-origin-isolated document before shared memory can be used.
Do not treat it like a transferable ArrayBuffer; sharing preserves access to the same memory instead of transferring ownership.
Concurrent non-atomic access can race, so synchronize shared data with suitable Atomics operations.

slice.summary: `String.prototype.slice()` returns a selected section of a string as a new string. The start is inclusive, the end is exclusive, and the original string remains unchanged.
slice.explanation: Call `slice()` on a string with a starting index and, optionally, an exclusive ending index. Negative indexes count backward from the end; the method returns a new string and does not change the original.

parameters.name: indexStart
parameters.description: The zero-based index of the first character included in the result. Negative values count backward from the string's end; omitted or nonnumeric values act as 0.

parameters.name: indexEnd
parameters.description: Optional zero-based index of the first character excluded from the result. Negative values count backward from the string's end; omitted or sufficiently large values select through the end.

slice.returns: A new string containing the extracted section of the string.

interview.question: What does String.prototype.slice() return, and does it mutate the source string?
interview.answer: `String.prototype.slice()` returns the selected portion as a new string. The start is included, while the end is excluded, and the original string is not modified.
interview.followUp: What does `slice(2, -1)` do? It starts at index 2 and stops before the final character after normalizing the negative end index.

interview.question: How are the start and end parameters interpreted?
interview.answer: The first parameter is the index of the first character to include. The optional second parameter is the index of the first character to exclude; omitting it extracts through the end.
interview.followUp: What happens when the end index is less than or equal to the start index? The method returns an empty string.

interview.question: How does slice() handle negative indexes?
interview.answer: A negative index is measured from the end of the string. If the start is negative, the effective start is the string length plus that value, with a lower bound of zero.
interview.followUp: What happens when the start is greater than or equal to the string length? The result is an empty string.

keyPoints: It creates a new string containing the selected section.
Calling the method leaves the source string unchanged.
`indexStart` identifies the first included character.
`indexEnd` is exclusive rather than inclusive.
An omitted, undefined, or sufficiently large end value selects the remainder.
gotchas: When the normalized end index is at or before the normalized start index, the result is an empty string.
A start index at or beyond the string length produces an empty string.
Negative start indexes count from the string's end, but values beyond the beginning are clamped to zero.

some.summary: `Array.prototype.some()` tests whether at least one array element satisfies a callback. It returns `true` on the first truthy result and otherwise returns `false`.
some.explanation: Call `some()` with a callback that tests each array element. It returns `true` as soon as the callback produces a truthy result; if every tested element produces a falsy result, it returns `false`.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as `this` when invoking `callbackFn`.

some.returns: A boolean: `true` when the callback returns a truthy value for at least one visited element; otherwise `false`.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.some() return and when does it stop?
interview.answer: `some()` returns a boolean indicating whether at least one array element makes the callback return a truthy value. It short-circuits and returns `true` immediately on the first match; otherwise it returns `false`.
interview.followUp: What happens for an empty array? It returns `false`, because no element can satisfy the predicate.

interview.question: What arguments can the callback receive?
interview.answer: The callback receives the current element, its index, and the array being traversed. An optional `thisArg` supplies the callback's `this` value.
interview.followUp: Does an arrow callback use `thisArg`? No. Arrow functions capture lexical `this`, so they do not rebind it from `thisArg`.

interview.question: How does some() handle sparse arrays and array-like objects?
interview.answer: `some()` invokes the callback only for indexes that have assigned values, so sparse-array holes are skipped. It is also generic: it only requires a `length` property and integer-keyed properties on its `this` value.
interview.followUp: Can it be used on an array-like object? Yes, when called generically, provided the object has the required length and integer-keyed properties.

keyPoints: Use `some()` to ask whether at least one array element passes a predicate.
The method short-circuits on the first successful test, avoiding unnecessary later callback calls.
A complete scan with no truthy callback result produces `false`.
The callback's first argument is the element currently being examined.
The callback's second argument is the current element's numeric index.
The callback's third argument is the array on which `some()` was invoked.
The method can operate on suitable array-like values, not only actual Array instances.
gotchas: The callback does not run for holes in a sparse array, so missing indexes are skipped rather than tested.

sort.summary: `Array.prototype.sort()` sorts an array in place and returns the same array. By default it compares string representations in UTF-16 order; pass a comparator for custom ordering.
sort.explanation: `sort()` rearranges an array's existing elements in place and returns that same array. With no comparator, it compares string representations in UTF-16 code-unit order; with a comparator, its numeric result determines which element comes first.

useCases.title: Locale-aware text order
useCases.scenario: Ordering text according to a locale by supplying a comparator such as one produced by `Intl.Collator`.

interview.question: Does `sort()` mutate the original array?
interview.answer: `sort()` mutates the array and returns a reference to that same, now-sorted array. It does not create a separate array.
interview.followUp: How would you sort without mutation? Use `toSorted()`, which returns a sorted copy while leaving the source array unchanged.

interview.question: What ordering does `sort()` use by default?
interview.answer: Without `compareFn`, elements are converted to strings and compared in UTF-16 code-unit order. Therefore, the default behavior is not numeric ordering for ordinary arrays.
interview.followUp: How do you sort numbers ascending? Pass `(a, b) => a - b` as the comparator.

interview.question: How does `compareFn` control ordering?
interview.answer: A comparator receives two defined elements, `a` and `b`. A negative result places `a` first, a positive result places `b` first, and zero or `NaN` treats them as equal.
interview.followUp: What happens to undefined elements? They are placed at the end without calling the comparator for them.

Leaving out the comparator triggers string conversion before comparison.
Default ordering follows character code-point values rather than numeric magnitude.
Return a negative comparator result to place the first argument before the second.
Return a positive comparator result to place the first argument after the second.
A zero or NaN comparator result treats the compared elements as equal in ordering.

The comparator is not invoked for undefined elements, and those elements always move to the end.

interview.answer: splice() mutates the receiver and returns an array containing the elements removed. Its arguments determine where changes begin, how many elements are removed, and which new elements are inserted.

interview.followUp: What happens when there are fewer substitutions than raw segments? Missing substitutions are treated as empty strings.

interview.question: What does String.raw return?
interview.answer: It returns the raw string form of the template literal. If the raw array-like object's length is non-positive, the result is the empty string.
interview.followUp: What happens to substitution values that are not strings? They are converted to strings during concatenation.

keyPoints: It is the standard built-in tag for reading template literal segments in raw form.
Expressions still evaluate, while backslash escape notation remains literal in the resulting string.
When called as an ordinary function, its first argument needs a raw property containing an array-like sequence of strings.
The trailing arguments supply the values placed between adjacent raw segments.
Its result is one string formed from raw segments and their substitutions.
The tagged-template form is the usual way to use this static method.
gotchas: A missing, zero, or negative raw length produces an empty string.

structuredClone.sourceTitle: Window: structuredClone () method - Web APIs | MDN
structuredClone.summary: structuredClone() creates a deep clone of a structured-cloneable JavaScript value. Its optional transfer list can move transferable resources into the clone instead of copying them.
structuredClone.explanation: structuredClone(value, options) recursively creates a structured clone of a supported value. With options.transfer, listed transferable resources move into the clone instead of being copied, leaving the original resources detached and unusable.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to clone; it must be structured-cloneable.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional options object. Its transfer property is an array of transferable objects to move rather than clone.

structuredClone.returns: A deep copy of the original value.

example.title: Deep-clone nested data
example.explanation: Creates an independent deep copy, including the nested object and Set.

useCases.title: Deep-copy application data
useCases.scenario: Create independent state snapshots containing nested objects, arrays, Maps, or Sets.

useCases.title: Transfer binary data efficiently
useCases.scenario: Move transferable resources such as an ArrayBuffer without duplicating their underlying storage.

useCases.title: Preserve circular references
useCases.scenario: Clone cyclic data structures that JSON serialization cannot represent.

interview.question: What does structuredClone do?
interview.answer: It creates a deep clone using the structured clone algorithm, so nested supported values are copied rather than shared. Unlike a shallow copy, changes to nested data in the result do not mutate the source.
interview.followUp: How are cycles handled? The algorithm keeps a map of previously visited references while recursing, allowing circular structures without infinite traversal.

interview.question: What are the parameters?
interview.answer: The first argument is the value to clone. The optional options object can contain transfer, an array of transferable objects that are moved instead of duplicated.
interview.followUp: What happens after transfer? The transferred resource is attached to the clone and detached from the original, so the source can no longer use it.

interview.question: What does it return, and when can it fail?
interview.answer: It returns a deep copy of the input value. If any part is not serializable, it throws a DataCloneError DOMException.
interview.followUp: Name two unsupported inputs. Functions and DOM nodes cannot be cloned by the structured clone algorithm.

keyPoints: It produces a deep clone rather than merely copying the top-level reference.
Circular object graphs are supported because previously encountered references are tracked during cloning.
The transfer option can move eligible resources instead of allocating a duplicate resource.
The input must be a value supported by the structured clone algorithm.
options.transfer identifies the transferable objects to move into the returned clone.
The return value is the independently cloned value.
gotchas: Functions cannot be cloned; attempting to clone one raises DataCloneError.
Custom prototypes are not preserved, so a cloned class instance does not retain its prototype behavior.
Descriptor metadata and accessor definitions are not reproduced in the clone.
A transferred resource is moved to the result; the corresponding resource in the input becomes unusable.

Symbol.summary: Symbol is a built-in function that creates unique, immutable primitive values. Symbols can serve as non-colliding object property keys, while Symbol.for() provides shared values through the global symbol registry.
Symbol.explanation: Symbol is a function-like built-in that creates an immutable primitive with unique identity. Use the resulting value as an object key when a property should not collide with string keys; use Symbol.for and Symbol.keyFor when sharing symbols through the global registry is required.

parameters.name: description
parameters.description: Optional text description associated with the symbol; it is used for display and does not determine uniqueness.

Symbol.returns: A new primitive value of type symbol.

example.title: Use a symbol as an object property key
example.explanation: A symbol creates a unique property key that can be used and later retrieved through the same symbol reference.

useCases.title: Collision-resistant object keys
useCases.scenario: Attach metadata or internal state to an object without competing with ordinary string property names.

useCases.title: Language protocol customization
useCases.scenario: Define protocol hooks recognized by JavaScript features, such as custom iteration behavior.

useCases.title: Cross-module or cross-realm coordination
useCases.scenario: Share a named symbol between code that uses the global symbol registry.

interview.question: What does Symbol() create, and are descriptions identity?
interview.answer: Symbol() creates a unique primitive symbol, optionally carrying a description. Each call has distinct identity, even when descriptions match.
interview.followUp: How can symbols be shared across realms? Use Symbol.for(key), which retrieves or creates a symbol in the global symbol registry.

interview.question: Why use a Symbol as an object property key?
interview.answer: A symbol can be used as an object property key, reducing accidental collisions with string-named properties. The same symbol reference is needed to access that property directly.
interview.followUp: How can symbol-keyed properties be discovered? Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(object) returns an array of the object's own symbol keys.

interview.question: Can Symbol be called with new?
interview.answer: Symbol is not constructible with new; attempting new Symbol() throws a TypeError. If an object wrapper is specifically needed, Object(symbol) creates one.
interview.followUp: How can the primitive and wrapper be distinguished? typeof the primitive is "symbol", while typeof its wrapper is "object".

keyPoints: Use symbols for property keys that should not collide with keys added by unrelated code.
A symbol key is distinct from every string key and from separately created symbols.
Call Symbol with an optional string description; the description helps debugging but does not establish identity.
typeof aSymbol returns "symbol", which identifies the primitive's type.
Use Object.getOwnPropertySymbols to enumerate an object's own symbol-keyed properties.
Use Symbol.for to obtain registry symbols and Symbol.keyFor to retrieve their registry keys.
gotchas: Symbol() returns a primitive, not a Symbol wrapper object.
Do not call Symbol with new; doing so throws a TypeError.
Calling Symbol repeatedly with the same description still produces different symbols.
Symbol.for uses registry identity, so it differs from creating a fresh symbol with Symbol().

trim.summary: trim() returns a new string with whitespace and line terminators removed from both ends of the string. It leaves the original string unchanged.
trim.explanation: Call trim() on a string to create a new string with whitespace and line terminators removed from its beginning and end. The method does not mutate the original string; if no trimming is needed, it still returns a new string.
trim.returns: A new string representing the input string with whitespace removed from its beginning and end.

example.title: Trim both ends of a string
example.explanation: This removes whitespace at both ends while leaving the original string unchanged.

useCases.title: Normalize input
useCases.scenario: Clean user-entered text before validation or storage.

useCases.title: Clean configuration values
useCases.scenario: Remove accidental surrounding whitespace from configuration or environment values.

useCases.title: Standardize text
useCases.scenario: Prepare text for reliable comparisons or display.

keyPoints: trim() removes surrounding whitespace at both ends and produces a new string.
Calling trim() does not change the string value on which it was called.
Use trimStart() for the beginning only or trimEnd() for the end only.
Its trimming set includes whitespace characters and line terminators.
Even an already-trimmed string results in a separate returned string value.
gotchas: The original string is not returned directly, even when it contains no surrounding whitespace.
The method removes both whitespace characters and line terminators, not merely ordinary spaces.

URL.summary: The URL interface parses, constructs, normalizes, and encodes URLs. It exposes URL components for inspection and modification, and can resolve relative references against a base URL.
URL.explanation: The URL interface parses and builds URL values while exposing their components as readable and writable properties. Create one with an absolute URL or resolve a relative reference against a base URL; use URLSearchParams through searchParams to manipulate its query.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: An absolute URL string or a relative reference to resolve against `base`.

parameters.name: base
parameters.description: The URL used to resolve a relative `url`; optional when `url` is absolute.

URL.returns: A URL object representing the resolved and parsed URL.

example.title: Resolve and modify a URL
example.explanation: Constructs an absolute URL from a relative path, adds a query parameter, and prints the serialized result.

useCases.title: Resolve relative URLs
useCases.scenario: Resolve route or asset references against a known origin or document URL.

useCases.title: Read and modify URL components
useCases.scenario: Inspect or update protocol, host, path, fragment, and query components.

useCases.title: Check URL validity
useCases.scenario: Validate URL input before attempting to use it.

useCases.title: Manage query parameters
useCases.scenario: Build and update query strings with structured parameter operations.

interview.question: How do you construct a URL from a relative path?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts an absolute URL, or a relative reference together with a base URL. It returns a URL object whose components can be inspected and changed.
interview.followUp: What happens if the input is relative and no base is supplied? Construction throws TypeError because the reference cannot be resolved.

interview.question: How can URL validity be checked before construction?
interview.answer: Use `URL.canParse(url, base)` when a boolean validity check is sufficient. Unlike construction, this static method reports whether the URL definition is parsable and valid.
interview.followUp: How can invalid input be represented without an exception? `URL.parse(url, base)` returns a URL object for valid input and `null` for invalid input.

interview.question: How should query parameters be modified?
interview.answer: The `searchParams` property exposes URLSearchParams for building and manipulating the query string. Methods such as `set()` update the URL's query parameters.
interview.followUp: How does direct query-string assignment differ? The `search` property represents the query string and setting it applies URL encoding rules.

keyPoints: URL provides one interface for parsing, constructing, normalizing, and encoding URL values.
Create an instance with `new URL()` and an absolute URL string.
A relative reference can be resolved by supplying a base URL.
`URL.canParse()` performs a non-throwing validity test and returns a boolean.
`URL.parse()` returns a URL object or `null` when the definition is invalid.
Properties expose URL components for reading and modification.
Use `URLSearchParams` through `searchParams` to work with query parameters.

URLSearchParams.summary: URLSearchParams provides utility methods for working with a URL's query string. Its iterable instances preserve ordered name-value pairs and can be modified or serialized.
URLSearchParams.explanation: Create an instance from a query string, iterable pairs, or a record, then use its methods to inspect or modify ordered name-value pairs. Serialization produces a URL-compatible query string, while iteration exposes the pairs in their existing order.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: A query string, an iterable of string pairs, or a record of string keys and values; the constructor argument is optional.

example.title: Read, modify, and serialize query parameters
example.explanation: Creates parameters from a query string, replaces duplicate tag values, adds a page parameter, reads values, and serializes the result.

useCases.title: Read query parameters
useCases.scenario: Parse incoming URL query data and retrieve one or multiple values by name.

useCases.title: Construct query strings
useCases.scenario: Build links or request URLs while safely encoding names and values.

useCases.title: Handle repeated parameters
useCases.scenario: Manage filters or selections represented by repeated query keys.

interview.question: What problem does URLSearchParams solve?
interview.answer: URLSearchParams represents URL query data as ordered name-value pairs. It can be constructed from a query string, iterable pairs, or a record, and it provides methods for reading, changing, iterating, and serializing those pairs.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve repeated keys? Use append() for each occurrence and getAll() when reading them, rather than set(), which removes other matching values.

interview.question: How do you handle duplicate query parameters?
interview.answer: get() returns the first value for a name, while getAll() returns every matching value in an array. has() tests whether a name or name-value pair exists.
interview.followUp: What happens when a name is absent? get() returns null, getAll() returns an empty array, and has() returns false.

interview.question: What is the difference between set() and append()?
interview.answer: set() assigns a value and removes additional values with the same name; it creates the parameter when none exists. append() always adds another name-value pair.
interview.followUp: How is the result encoded? toString() applies application/x-www-form-urlencoded encoding and represents spaces as plus signs.

keyPoints: The class provides a standard API for parsing, querying, editing, and serializing URL query data.
Instances support direct for...of iteration without first calling entries().
Iteration preserves the input order of the parameter pairs.
append() preserves existing values and adds another pair, making it suitable for repeated keys.
set() replaces the value associated with a name and creates the name if it is absent.
sort() orders the parameter list by key when canonical ordering is needed.
gotchas: When constructing from a string, an initial question mark is optional and is discarded.
Only the string constructor form performs percent-decoding and converts plus signs to spaces.
Record input accepts only flat string-key and string-value data; nested structures are not represented.

WeakMap.summary: WeakMap stores values using objects or non-registered symbols as keys without strongly retaining those keys. It is useful for object-associated data that should disappear as the key becomes unreachable.
WeakMap.explanation: A WeakMap stores values under object or non-registered symbol keys while avoiding strong references to those keys. It supports querying, retrieval, insertion, and deletion, but does not expose key enumeration because garbage collection can change which keys remain live.

example.title: Associating metadata with an object
example.explanation: A WeakMap associates metadata with an object without keeping that object alive solely because it is a key.

useCases.title: Object-associated metadata
useCases.scenario: Attach metadata, caches, or private state to objects without making the objects stay alive solely because of that association.

useCases.title: Weakly retained caches
useCases.scenario: Keep computed information for object keys while allowing entries to become collectible when those keys are no longer used.

useCases.title: Encapsulated object state
useCases.scenario: Hide implementation details behind object identity rather than exposing an ordinary property on the object.

interview.question: What distinguishes WeakMap from Map?
interview.answer: WeakMap holds key/value pairs without strongly retaining its object keys. If a key becomes otherwise unreachable, it may be garbage collected, and its associated value can then become collectible too.
interview.followUp: Why is WeakMap not iterable? Because garbage collection can remove keys at nondeterministic times, exposing enumeration would make the observable result depend on garbage-collection state.

interview.question: What keys and operations does WeakMap support?
interview.answer: WeakMap keys must be objects or non-registered symbols, while values may have any JavaScript type. Operations such as get, set, has, and delete work with a particular key, but there is no operation to list all keys.
interview.followUp: When would a Map be preferable? Use Map when keys must be enumerable or when primitive keys such as strings and numbers are needed.

interview.question: When is WeakMap useful in application design?
interview.answer: A common use is attaching private or implementation-specific data to objects. The data remains associated with the object while it is reachable, without requiring a separate cleanup step when the object is collected.
interview.followUp: How can object identity affect this pattern? A newly created object with the same properties is still a different key, so callers must retain and reuse the original reference.

keyPoints: Keys are restricted to objects and non-registered symbols.
Values can be primitives, objects, functions, or any other JavaScript value.
Storing a key does not by itself prevent that key from being garbage collected.
When a key is collected, its corresponding WeakMap value can become eligible for collection if nothing else retains it.
WeakMap deliberately has no key-list or enumeration method.
gotchas: Primitive keys are generally invalid; the supported primitive exception is a non-registered symbol.

WeakRef.summary: WeakRef provides a non-owning reference to an object or non-registered symbol, so the target may be garbage-collected. Use deref() to retrieve the target when it is still available; garbage-collection timing is nondeterministic.
WeakRef.explanation: WeakRef holds a non-owning reference to an object or non-registered symbol. Calling deref() retrieves the target while it remains available, or returns undefined after garbage collection; collection timing is nondeterministic.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The value to reference; it must be an object or a non-registered symbol.

WeakRef.returns: A new WeakRef object referring to the supplied target; deref() returns the target or undefined if it has been reclaimed.

example.title: Safely dereference a target
example.explanation: Creates a weak reference and safely uses the target only when dereferencing still returns it.

useCases.title: Memory-sensitive caches
useCases.scenario: Cache large objects without making the cache a strong owner of their memory.

useCases.title: Non-owning object tracking
useCases.scenario: Track optional objects such as DOM nodes without preventing their collection.

useCases.title: Ephemeral associations
useCases.scenario: Access a resource only while its target remains alive, with a fallback when deref() returns undefined.

keyPoints: WeakRef observes a target without keeping it alive.
The target may be an object or a non-registered symbol.
The target can disappear when no strong references remain, but collection is optional.
deref() returns the target when available and undefined after reclamation.
The referenced value is called the target or referent.
gotchas: Do not use deref() as a deterministic signal that garbage collection has occurred.
A WeakRef cannot be retargeted after construction.

WeakSet.summary: WeakSet is a collection of unique objects and non-registered symbols held weakly, so unreachable members may be garbage-collected. It supports membership checks and mutation but cannot be enumerated.
WeakSet.explanation: WeakSet stores unique objects and non-registered symbols through weak references. It supports adding, checking, and deleting individual values, while intentionally providing no enumeration mechanism, so values can become garbage-collectable when nothing else strongly references them.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: Optional iterable whose elements are added to the new WeakSet. Each element must be an object or a non-registered symbol; null is treated as undefined.

example.title: Track object identity
example.explanation: The set tracks the first object by identity; a separate object with identical contents is not the same value.

useCases.title: Non-retaining object tagging
useCases.scenario: Track whether objects have already been processed without extending their lifetime.

useCases.title: Garbage-collection-friendly state
useCases.scenario: Associate temporary membership with objects in caches or lifecycle-sensitive workflows.

useCases.title: Visited-object tracking
useCases.scenario: Prevent repeated handling of object references during graph or tree traversal.

interview.question: What makes WeakSet different from Set?
interview.answer: WeakSet is useful when membership should not keep an object alive. Its references are weak, so an object may be garbage-collected when no other strong references remain.
interview.followUp: How can code detect when an unreferenced member has been collected? It cannot observe that directly, because WeakSet deliberately has no enumeration or size mechanism.

interview.question: Which values can a WeakSet contain, and how are they compared?
interview.answer: WeakSet accepts objects and non-registered symbols, stores each value at most once, and compares objects by identity rather than by their contents.
interview.followUp: What happens with two separately created objects containing the same properties? They are distinct references, so both can be members.

interview.question: Which operations does WeakSet provide?
interview.answer: The main instance operations are add(), has(), and delete(). add() returns the WeakSet, has() returns a boolean, and delete() removes a matching value.
interview.followUp: What does has() return for a primitive or registered symbol? It returns false rather than treating that value as a valid member.

keyPoints: Its element type is restricted to garbage-collectable objects and non-registered symbols.
Adding the same object repeatedly does not create duplicate membership.
Weak membership allows otherwise unreachable objects to be reclaimed.
Membership uses SameValueZero semantics; for supported object values, identity determines equality.
Two separate objects with identical properties remain different WeakSet elements.
add(value) inserts a supported value and returns the WeakSet instance.
gotchas: You cannot iterate over a WeakSet or inspect its size; use has() when you already have a candidate value.
Calling WeakSet() as a function throws a TypeError; create instances with new WeakSet().
